articles.full_text:
CBAM: how the EU aims to strengthen the ‘carbon border adjustment mechanism’
Brussels wants to extend the levy on non-EU polluting products to downstream goods such as household appliances and cars
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the “tCO2 tax at the borders”, designed to ensure fair competition between European and non-EU producers ahead of the reform of the ETS (Emissions Trading System), is now in its first year of operation.
It has been a challenging year, which officially began on 1 January with many pieces still missing – pieces which – only in these final months of 2026 – are falling into place to lead to define the overall framework in the coming weeks (14 guidelines published at the end of August, the register beginning to take shape, accredited verifiers only available from September, a number of regulations still missing, and so on). Nevertheless, there is already talk of an extension.
Balancing the market
The EU’s new own resource is designed to apply to imports a levy based on the incremental cost that European producers of ‘polluting’ goods at risk of relocation will have to bear in the coming years, given the phasing out of the free allowances from which they have benefited up to and including 2025.
If, therefore, European manufacturers are paying (and will continue to pay) ever more to produce ‘polluting’ goods, it becomes essential to introduce – in parallel – an equivalent levy on non-EU manufacturers wishing to access our market: this, in fact, is the CBAM.
The transitional period, which began in the final quarter of 2023 and ended at the end of 2025, served as a test bed for the system: it enabled stakeholders to come to terms with the measure, come to terms with its impacts but, above all, to assess its effectiveness, highlighting both its practical challenges and benefits.

A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers urged President Donald Trump on Sept. 29 not to ease sanctions against Russia, amid reports that his administration is considering sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners.
Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley, along with Republicans Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, called on the administration to maintain pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers' statement comes as Washington considers using sanctions relief as leverage to encourage Russia to take steps toward ending the war.
The proposal, first reported by the Atlantic and confirmed to the Kyiv Independent by people familiar with the matter, would involve pressing Moscow to release political prisoners in exchange for easing sanctions and restoring some economic ties with Russia.
"Sanctions relief will embolden Russia and prolong the war," the lawmakers said.
The representatives also pointed to legislation that Congress recently passed, which significantly expands U.S. sanctions authority against Russia.
"Two weeks ago, Congress passed the most significant Russia sanctions legislation since 2017," they said. "We look forward to the Administration's first round of new sanctions designations ahead of Oct. 18, the first deadline in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act."
The legislation, spearheaded by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham and signed by Trump on Sept. 19, authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil.
The U.S. president said on Sept. 22 that he would use the tariff authorities granted by the legislation if necessary to help end Russia's war against Ukraine.
The debate over sanctions relief comes as Russia's economy faces mounting pressure from long-term Western restrictions. Sanctions relief has become one of Moscow's main objectives, while some U.S. officials see easing sanctions as an incentive for Russia to agree to a ceasefire.
The latest push comes as Washington seeks to revive efforts to end the war. Those efforts stalled earlier this year amid Russia's territorial demands and the U.S.-Iran war.
Moscow has continued its attacks against Ukraine while clearly showing no indication that it is prepared to accept a ceasefire or make concessions in negotiations.

articles.title: Google appeals two European Commission Digital Markets Act decisions to the General Court - Digital Watch Observatory
articles.summary: Google appeals two European Commission Digital Markets Act decisions to the General Court  Digital Watch Observatory
articles.full_text:
Google filed appeals with the EU General Court against two European Commission decisions under the Digital Markets Act.
Google has filed an appeal with the General Court of the European Union, against two decisions of the European Commission issued under the Digital Markets Act (DMA). The appeals concern a decision that set a January 2027 deadline for Google to share search data with third‑party search engines and a decision that gave the company until July 2027 to make changes to the Android operating system.
In July, the European Commission said Google should take steps to ensure that rival artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can access the same features on Android devices as Google’s own assistant and that users be able to activate their preferred AI assistant via voice commands, for example to book a taxi. The Commission also requested that Google share search data with designated third‑party search engines, including AI chatbots, to enable them to compete more fairly with Google Search and to give users in Europe a broader range of options. The requests were issued as binding obligations under the DMA, which designates Alphabet as a ‘gatekeeper’ and requires gatekeepers to guarantee interoperability and to refrain from treating their own services more favourably or tracking users outside their platform without consent.
In a statement issued to the media, Google added that the decision on search data sharing would require the company to pass ‘sensitive data to commercial entities without sufficient protections, user knowledge, or consent’ and that granting ‘powerful permissions on Android to downloaded apps that haven’t been vetted by phone makers’ poses threats to device security.
According to Luxembourg Times, Oliver Bethell, senior director of competition at Google, said the company was ‘appealing decisions that will force us to share people’s private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken vital security protections on Android’.
On the other hand, a European Commission spokeswoman said the bloc would defend its decisions in court and stated that the requests had been made after ‘carefully considered integrity and security with respect to the features involved as well as the protection of personal data’.
In a separate undertaking, Google announced on 8 September that it had implemented a new layout for its online search results in Europe, in response to the EU’s July finding. The current appeal by Google allows it to object to some requirements, that it argues will result in sharing user data and opening Android’s core architecture, while still implementing other changes.
Why does it matter?
The dispute concerns the application of the DMA’s obligations on Google as a designated gatekeeper. The European Commission uses ongoing regulatory dialogue with digital gatekeepers, as a means of monitoring, influencing, and ensuring compliance with the DMA. As a result, Google implemented certain structural amendments on 8 September in order to come into compliance.
Google has also now appealed other decisions of the Commission arguing on the issue of the integrity and security of personal data that it is being asked to share. At the same time, the Commission considers data sharing to be crucial for the development and optimisation of third-party search engines, and will help to create a more level playing field. At the core of the Commission’s decision is Google’s dominant position in the search engine market which is as a result of its access to a wealth of user data, which it uses to improve its search algorithm.

The United States on Thursday urged European allies to release strategic diesel reserves immediately to curb prices driven higher by the US war on Iran. EU states will discuss a coordinated response on Friday, as Washington increases pressure following President Donald Trump's suggestion that he could ban US diesel exports.
The United States on Thursday told its European allies to help lower global diesel prices by releasing strategic reserves "immediately," with EU member states due to discuss the crisis on Friday.
Reports said the Trump administration wants France and Germany in particular to tap their stockpiles of diesel to try to curb prices sent soaring by the US war on Iran.
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a post on social media.
EU member states will meet with the European Commission Friday to discuss a coordinated response to soaring fuel prices, a Commission spokesman said.
Washington is piling on pressure to get European help with fuel costs, with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday floating the possibility of banning diesel exports.
High energy costs loom as a threat to Trump's Republican party in next month's midterm elections.
"It is in Europe's best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers," a US official told AFP.
At G20 trade talks in Milwaukee, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer struck a conciliatory tone, saying there was an "eagerness on both sides to work together" on the diesel issue.
And Trump told reporters in Texas on Thursday that he "may" ask European countries to release diesel reserves.
Read moreTrump sparks debate over diesel export ban
'Unexpected'
Still, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters Thursday that any move by the US to ban diesel exports would be "unexpected for Europeans."
He spoke on the sidelines of the two-day G20 trade ministers' gathering in Milwaukee, after meeting with Greer.
Sefcovic told reporters that he did not go into details with Greer on energy exports.
But the transatlantic partners "decided to stay in close touch to avoid any surprises here," he said.
"It would have very dramatic consequences for our economic performance," Sefcovic said of any potential diesel export ban.
France's minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier, told AFP in Milwaukee: "I can't imagine that there will be a ban."
He stressed the importance of diesel to the United States and European countries, adding both sides will "try to find solutions."
"In France, we'll try to find balanced solutions all over the world," Forissier added. "If not with the Americans, it will be with other countries."
Trump on Wednesday said he was still considering a possible ban on US diesel exports, while adding that he thought it could ultimately cause gasoline prices to rise.
"I'm thinking about it," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Speaking alongside Trump, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Wednesday that the world would "hear announcements from our friends in Europe" to push diesel prices down.
Asked about a release from strategic reserves, the French presidency said no such demand had been made when Emmanuel Macron and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last week.
Macron would also soon convene a video meeting of G7 leaders "to make progress on the various levers that can be used to address the rising fuel prices... including coordination on releasing reserves."
Macron announced on September 18 a plan for such a meeting. The G7 gathering is expected in mid-October, according to Macron's press office.
Average US diesel prices have surged more than 70 percent to $6.39 a gallon since the start of the Iran war, according to AAA motor club data.
Fuel prices have caused living costs to soar, leaving Trump's Republican Party fearing it could lose control of Congress in November's midterm elections.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.summary: CBAM: dialogue with suppliers is crucial for businesses  Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.full_text:
To measure costs, we need accurate data throughout the production chain
From 1 January 2026, CBAM will require the establishment of a comprehensive internal process, to be developed in advance, in a manner appropriate to the impacts in terms of costs, risks and administrative burdens on individual organisations.
Impact assessment
The first area concerns the impact assessment. Businesses will need to calculate the cost of the CBAM on imported products by simulating the effects of applying default values or, where practicable, actual values. Comparing the two scenarios will be essential to understanding the potential cost of the mechanism. For default values, the exercise is simpler, as it is sufficient to apply the parameters provided by the Commission (which, incidentally, have recently been updated and corrected). A critical point: the definition of the non-preferential origin of goods in accordance with the relevant rules laid down by EU legislation.
We know, however, that default values provide inaccurate data. By contrast, actual values require a great deal of effort: in fact, the operator of the non-EU production plant must commit to establishing a proper procedure for monitoring and verification, promptly engaging an accredited verifier, and organising site visits and checks in good time for the 30 September reporting deadline.
It has only been possible to obtain the qualification of accredited verifier since 1 September (as at 24 September, there was only one registered verifier), and it was only last August that the Commission’s Guidance for non-EU operators and verifiers was published. In other words, anyone wishing to obtain the 2026 emissions certification in good time will have to act quickly.
Costs to be set aside
At the same time, from 1 January 2026, the issue of provisioning for the CBAM cost in the accounts will need to be addressed, and it will be necessary to determine, on a case-by-case basis, whether it is possible to use the present values that have not yet been certified.

articles.title: France meets fiscal reality with a crunch - Financial Times
articles.summary: France meets fiscal reality with a crunch  Financial TimesFrance seeks to rein in pensions and state salaries in 2027  Financial TimesFiscal troubles for the euro may only be starting  ING ThinkFrench government's draft budget relies on tax hikes to take back control over public finances  Le Monde.frBond markets whack France for fiscal irresponsibility  The Economist
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
“Reality is catching up with us,” French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned this week on the eve of presenting the 2027 budget. Lecornu was referring to this year’s surge in government borrowing costs which aggravates France’s fiscal woes just as it enters the presidential election campaign. Amid a broader debt market sell-off, France has become a focal point of investor jitters about debt sustainability.
France’s debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at 119 per cent. Its 10-year bond yields this week climbed above 4.9 per cent, the highest in the Eurozone, from 3.6 per cent in early July. The premium that Paris must pay compared with German debt has risen sharply to more than 125 basis points, the highest level since the peak of the Eurozone crisis in 2012. A country that has not run a budget surplus since 1974 is now paying dearly for its profligacy.
The draft budget would make total savings of €54bn next year, including €43bn of new measures, in a mixture of tax rises and spending cuts. That should be enough to trim the deficit from 5.4 per cent to 5 per cent, a target France was supposed to hit in 2026 but, as in so many previous years, has missed. Lecornu’s minority government could push the budget through by decree, at the risk of being toppled in a censure vote, but the plan will soon be overtaken by next spring’s presidential vote. Investors are paying less attention to a temporary fix at the tail-end of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency and more to the political and fiscal developments that follow. They don’t like what they see.
The first concern is the structural deterioration in the public finances. On current policies, the deficit would hit 6.8 per cent by 2030, according to a government-appointed commission, as spending is driven up by population ageing and rising interest costs. Debt servicing would eat up €124bn in 2030, the commission estimated, 60 per cent more than France’s defence spending.
The second worry is the inability of France’s political class to find some kind of majority for fiscal retrenchment. As the election campaign begins, the populists have the momentum while a divided centre is struggling to gain traction. It has become impossible for candidates to ignore France’s debt problem, but their answers mostly lack credibility. Whoever wins the presidency may not secure a majority in follow-up parliamentary elections, meaning more political deadlock.
The worst-case scenario for debt investors would be a run-off between the far-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the far-right Marine Le Pen. Mélenchon has proposed cancelling government debt held by France’s central bank, which would send fear rippling across debt markets. Le Pen has committed to a 3 per cent deficit ceiling but lacks anything like a serious plan for the €140bn or so in annual savings needed to get there by 2032.
The centre-left wants to pile more taxes on businesses and the wealthy despite the inevitable hit to investment and jobs. Thankfully, Édouard Philippe, the leading centrist candidate, injected some sanity into the race this week by proposing to raise the retirement age to 65 and the contribution period for a full pension to 45 years. It is only a start, but a bold gamble in the current climate.
Since France is too big to fail, investors expect the European Central Bank to eventually intervene in case of crisis, keeping a lid on yields. The ECB has the tools and could step in to prevent contagion to other Eurozone sovereigns. But it would also face stiff opposition in other capitals to bailing out a country that has repeatedly failed to get its house in order, especially if led by a president who is at loggerheads with the EU on other fronts. The market squeeze and France’s fiscal pain could get much worse before any rescue.

articles.summary: Escalating nuclear threats and a Brexit rethink  Euronews.comPutin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad  BBCPutin warns West that Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons’ to protect Kaliningrad  CNNRussia sends nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic  ReutersPutin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Good morning, I’m Mared Gwyn. Welcome to your Thursday newsletter. Today: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte tells Euronews that Russia should stop issuing nuclear threats, and the UK Prime Minister puts EU membership back on the table.
Nuclear tensions: In an interview with Euronews, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has told Russia to stop issuing nuclear threats, after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance saying it is prepared to deploy its nuclear arsenal if its territory – including the enclave of Kaliningrad – comes under attack.
‘Stop’: "We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," Rutte exclusively told the Euronews Defence and Space Summit on Wednesday, at a moment of heightened tension between Russia and the West.
Rutte, however, dismissed the immediate threat to the alliance’s members, saying "we will defend every inch of NATO territory”.
“That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he explained.
Reuters first reported that Russia had warned NATO in a document that it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to annex the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, while also threatening strikes on “decision-making centres” in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.
‘Worst-case scenario’: Earlier on Wednesday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev – also speaking at Euronews’ summit – called for European dialogue with Russia to avert a nuclear attack. While rejecting the Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric, Radev reminded his European counterparts of the “nuclear card”, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered.
"We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation,” Radev said.
Making Putin feel that ‘war is coming’: The European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius, rejectedRadev’s call for diplomatic engagement, warning it could embolden President Putin and undermine Ukraine.
"Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender - that is their diplomacy position," Kubilius told Euronews, adding that Putin needs to “feel that war is coming to Russia itself”.
‘Made in Europe’ under fire: A push from Brussels to prioritise domestic European companies in defence contracts was also front and centre of the debate on Wednesday. NATO chief Rutte described the debate as a “luxury”, warning that the initiative ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough.
Earlier on Wednesday, the US Ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, slammed the EU’s “Buy European” weapons push as “self-interest”, saying it could disrupt the transatlantic defence industrial base and benefit Europe’s "enemies".
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics," Puzder told the summit audience.
My colleagues and I have more takeaways from the summit for you inthis debrief.
Migration talks: Home Affairs Ministers are meeting in Luxembourg with migration top of the agenda. Ministers are expected to discuss proposed measures to tackle irregular arrivals under the European Emergency Response Framework, expected to be unveiled by the Commission next month.
EU sources tell my colleague Vincenzo Genovese that the proposal is expected to include a temporary suspension of asylum rights.
Italy extends border controls: The meeting comes as tensions between Italy and Spain escalate again, after Rome extended aerial and maritime border checks with Spain by another 15 days in response to the situation in the enclave of Ceuta, where 80,000 migrants entered in an unprecedented mass entry in July.
Meanwhile, a delegation of MEPs visited the Spanish exclave on Wednesday, denouncing the attacks and smear campaigns directed against activists and organisations working on the ground by far-right groups.
French and Spanish leaders welcome Andy Burnham’s suggestion UK could go ‘all the way’ and rejoin the EU
French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could look to rejoin the EU, with Macron saying “welcome back” when asked about the prospect during a press conference in Madrid.
“If the British want to come back and if the Prime Minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans,” Macron said, speaking alongside Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who also said the UK would be welcome back in the bloc.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday floated going “all the way” and rejoining the EU, as he vowed to scope out options for future EU-UK ties.
“We could stay as we are. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said about the (EU) single market, or we could go all the way," Burnham said.
The UK leader also said that the EU-UK summit postponed in July amid Starmer’s resignation would be held in November.
Burnham has so far been perceived as much less focused on international and EU affairs than his predecessor Keir Starmer, leaving EU officials second-guessing his intentions for resetting relations with the bloc. articles.summary: Digital Markets Guide - Sixth Edition - European Union: regulating Big Tech in the age of AI  Global Competition Review
articles.full_text:
This is an Insight article, written by a selected contributor as part of GCR's co-published content. Learn more about Insight
Overview
Regulators in Europe addressed the inadequacy of traditional competition law in dealing with the challenges created by the rapid pace of development in the digital era and increasing market power of certain gatekeepers. The Digital Markets Act (DMA)[1]and Digital Services Act (DSA),[2]containing detailed duties for gatekeepers and digital services entering into effect in 2024, were implemented. To safeguard the effectiveness of the new laws, both the European Commission and certain national authorities were granted additional enforcement powers and resources.
The European Commission has clearly signalled, both in advance and by actually enforcing the new laws, its intention to safeguard compliance with this new digital legislation rigorously and to deploy the full range of instruments available to it. This is evidenced by a series of informal and formal investigations into potential infringements of the DMA that the Commission has already launched and concluded.
On top of that, the economy is in an AI boom, which again brings new legal challenges in ensuring fair and open markets. The Commission therefore introduced the AI Act,[3]the first legal framework to address and regulate AI. However, while certain provisions of the AI Act have become active already in 2025, the recent Digital Omnibus will lead to a delay of the application of certain rules and to further changes to the overall framework. Activities in the field of AI are, however, not confined to new regulation. The Commission has also opened investigations under article 102 TFEU into newly emerging AI services like Google's "AI Overviews" and "AI Mode", which make use of third-party content and may foreclose competitors.[4]Only recently, the Commission has issued interim measures against Meta and its plan to ban certain third-party AI features from WhatsApp.
The new regimes have encouraged vivid private and public enforcement and thus pulled the reins for gatekeepers tight:
- Countless complainants addressed antitrust and DMA concerns to the competent authorities. Authorities and the accused companies engage in informal discussions to avoid lengthy investigations and remedy, as the case may be, violations through commitments or settlements, most prominently in the "regulatory dialogue" with the Commission on DMA compliance.
- National laws allow for the private enforcement of claims for injunctions or damages so that affected companies can bring to an end DMA or antitrust violations not only through raising complaints with the competition authorities, but also themselves by claiming injunctions and damages before the competent national courts. That said, following the wave of follow-on cartel damage cases, increasing follow-on and stand-alone damages claims as well as claims for injunctions were filed, among others in Germany where, to the extent publicly known, the first cease and desist order by a national court was handed down ordering Google to cease and desist from an EU wide DMA violation.
- Cases affect a wide area of business models, reaching from platform services in the sense of the DMA, cloud and AI services (eg, the Commission's antitrust investigations against Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode), online advertising and publishing, or to data protection, with concerns over self-preferencing, market foreclosure, user consent, excessive fees and technical barriers.
- Authorities are also broadening their scope and theories of harm in merger control, using tools to capture below-threshold deals, analysing ecosystem effects and raising vertical foreclosure concerns.
DMA and DSA
The DMA and DSA entered into force on 1 November 2022 and have applied as of 2 May 2023, resulting in a transformation of the EU's digital regulatory environment, with the aim of creating a "safer digital space in which the fundamental rights of all users of digital services are protected" and "a level playing field to foster innovation, growth and competitiveness, both in the European Single Market and globally".[5]
With the most important provisions of the DMA and DSA being applicable as of 2023–2024, the past two years have brought many notable developments in the EU's digital sector.
Digital Markets Act
Background
With the DMA, the EU legislator pursues competition policy concerns that are specific to digital markets. The DMA is based on the realisation that although traditional antitrust law, in particular article 102 TFEU, applies in the digital economy, it is not suitable for protecting digital markets from monopolisation and for keeping them open. To protect, or partially restore the openness of markets, the EU legislator considered it necessary to subject the competitive power of gatekeepers to a specific regulatory regime.
The DMA sets out specific obligations that apply to certain core platform services (CPS) offered by large digital companies that are identified as gatekeepers through thresholds[6] and other metrics. At the heart of the DMA is a catalogue of obligations (in particular articles 5, 6, 7 and 13(4) DMA) for those undertakings that have been designated as gatekeepers by the Commission, and which provide core platform services such as search engines, operating systems, browsers, intermediation services like marketplaces, or certain communication services and can thereby control or influence the competitive conditions on adjacent markets (article 2 No. 2 and article 3 DMA). The DMA shall prevent gatekeepers from exploiting their market power in favour of their own offers and to the detriment of competitors and platform users. According to article 1(1) DMA, the purpose of the DMA is:
to contribute to the proper functioning of the internal market by laying down harmonised rules ensuring for all businesses, contestable and fair markets in the digital sector across the Union where gatekeepers are present, to the benefit of business users and end users.
Unlike in antitrust law, the application of the obligations under the DMA does not require a complex delineation of relevant markets or the weighing of competitive concerns and legitimate interests in individual cases. The legislator introduced “per se rules”, that are not open to case-by-case impact analyses but must be complied with unconditionally after being designated as a gatekeeper. This is a deliberate decision of the legislator, which is intended, in particular, to ensure swift enforcement in individual cases to prevent gatekeepers from continuing to harm competition during lengthy (antitrust) proceedings.
Following extensive discussions with potential gatekeepers regarding thresholds and designation, on 6 September 2023, the Commission designated six companies as gatekeepers: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft. On 13 May 2024, the Commission also designated Booking.
Initial designations and market investigations
In total, 23 CPSs have been listed in individual designation decisions.

| Intermediation services | Google Maps, Google Play, Google Shopping, Amazon Marketplace, App Store, Booking.com | 
| Ads | Google, Amazon, Meta | 
| Browser | Chrome, Safari | 
| Operating System | Google Android, iOS, iPad OS, Windows PC OS | 
| Video Sharing | YouTube | 
| Search | Google Search | 
| Messaging services | WhatsApp, Messenger |

Nevertheless, some services managed to successfully avoid a CPS designation by arguing that they do not constitute an important gateway for business users to reach end users. Gmail and Outlook, for example, were not designated as they do not impose any significant degree of dependency between business users and end users, as they allow users to exchange messages with users of any other email service. Samsung's Internet Browser bypassed the designation due to low and declining market share combined with the lack of strength of Samsung's wider ecosystem. articles.title: Overview of EU and UK Regulatory Developments relating to Autonomous Vehicles - Inside Global Tech
articles.summary: Overview of EU and UK Regulatory Developments relating to Autonomous Vehicles  Inside Global Tech
articles.full_text:
Driverless and autonomous vehicles (“AVs”) are moving from test tracks and pilot schemes to commercial deployment around the world. In the U.S. and China, robotaxi fleets and autonomous trucking services are proliferating. Similar developments are happening in the EU and UK. In London, the first commercial autonomous ride-hailing service launched in early September 2026, with a supervised fleet carrying paying passengers. In Germany, regulators have granted the first nationwide authorisations for Level 4 urban testing and cab-less Level 4 autonomous trucks. At the international level, UNECE has adopted the first global rules for fully driverless vehicles, as discussed in our earlier blog post here.
As AV technology matures, the regulatory and liability frameworks that will govern it are starting to emerge. This article provides an overview of the key developments that will affect autonomous vehicle manufacturers, and technology companies and mobility-service providers operating in this sector.
Current State of AV Deployment
In the EU, 18 Member States signed a Joint Declaration of Intent in June 2026 on large-scale cross-border testbeds for autonomous vehicles, under the European Automotive Action Plan. In Germany, the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) granted nationwide authorisation in July 2026 for Level 4 automated-driving testing on urban roads — the first such nationwide urban approval, allowing testing across German cities without a separate authorisation process required in each location.
In the UK, the Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services) Regulations 2026 came into force on 15 May 2026, creating a clear framework and dedicated portal for companies to obtain permits to offer automated passenger services. The portal is now open. As of late September 2026, no operator has yet completed the relevant vehicle-registration stage or applied for a driverless permit – we continue to monitor this space. Separately, the UK Department for Transport’s consultation on a draft Statement of Safety Principles for automated vehicles, which will set the safety-related benchmarks for automated vehicles, closed on 9 September 2026.
London’s first commercial autonomous ride-hailing service launched in early September 2026. This currently operates with a trained, Transport for London (TfL)-licensed driver on board to monitor trips and intervene if necessary. These services run under the ordinary private-hire licensing framework rather than the new driverless permit scheme.
Implementing the UNECE Framework for Automated Driving Systems
In June 2026, UNECE’s World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations (“WP.29”) adopted the first international regulatory framework for fully driverless Automated Driving Systems (“ADS”), comprising a new UN Regulation (“UNR”), and a companion Global Technical Regulation (“GTR”). For more information, see our earlier blog post here.
Following adoption of the UNR on ADS, the European Commission is preparing a delegated regulation to amend the annexes to the General Safety Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, which is likely to incorporate the new UN ADS Regulation. Commission adoption is currently planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.
The UK’s plans for adopting the UNR on ADS is less clear at this stage. The UK Department for Transport’s August 2026 consultation on GB type approval (which closed on 29 September) does not propose incorporating the UN ADS Regulation into the domestic framework.
Liability Framework
As AVs move from test tracks to public roads, the question of who bears liability when something goes wrong remains top of mind for legislators, regulators and industry stakeholders. The EU’s recent reform of its product liability framework will directly affect companies supplying autonomous-driving software and AI, and similar changes may be to come in the UK.
The EU is already ahead of the UK in this area, having adopted a major reform of its product liability framework through the revised Product Liability Directive (“PLD”). Although already adopted, the revised PLD applies only to products placed on the market or put into service from 9 December 2026. The revised PLD modernises EU product liability law by expressly bringing software within scope, whether supplied on a standalone basis or integrated into a product. This is particularly significant for autonomous vehicles, where liability exposure may extend beyond the physical vehicle to autonomous-driving software and AI-enabled driving functions. In addition, certain related digital services may themselves fall within scope, including, for example, services providing the continuous supply of traffic or navigation data. The PLD must be transposed into national law by 9 December 2026. Transposition is underway and divergences are already emerging (creating uncertainty and scope for satellite litigation). The Commission has also been engaging with Member States on implementation issues as the date of application approaches. (For more information on the PLD, see our client alert here, and our blog post here on PLD transposition.)
Meanwhile, a cross-party group of senior MEPs has reportedly recently urged the EU Commission to consider new specific AI liability legislation to address perceived gaps in the framework for harms caused by advanced AI systems, following the formal withdrawal in 2025 of the proposed AI Liability Directive.
In the UK, the Jurisdiction Taskforce (“UKJT”) recently analyzed the current provision for allocation of responsibility for AI-related harms, concluding that existing English law principles (e.g., contract, negligence and, to a lesser extent, statutory strict liability) are generally capable of allocating responsibility without a new bespoke regime. The statement includes an AV-specific illustration, suggesting that existing principles of contributory negligence could be applied to reduce liability where an AI system recommended a driving route across soft tidal sands and a user crossed the beach knowing the hazard. The statement is non-binding but likely to be of persuasive value (the UKJT’s membership includes respected academics and members of the judiciary).
However, the UK Law Commission is actively reviewing the current product liability regime with a view to making recommendations for reform, and has AI clearly in its sights. It considers the current regime to be no longer fit for purpose, and is considering options to modernise the law, including to account for emerging technologies, including AI. The review is considering whether to introduce similar claimant-friendly reforms to those in the new PLD. Its proposals for reform are expected to be published for consultation before the end of 2026.
Next Steps
The remainder of 2026 appears likely to be a defining period for AV regulation in the EU and UK. In the EU, the Commission’s delegated regulation incorporating the UNECE driverless framework into the General Safety Regulation is expected in Q4, while the deadline for Member State transposition of the revised Product Liability Directive is 9 December.
In the UK, the Department for Transport has promised a further consultation in the second half of 2026 on the Automated Vehicles Act secondary legislation, covering authorisation, operator licensing, safety principles and data access. The Law Commission’s product liability reform proposals are expected before year-end. On the deployment side, permits for the first automated passenger-services and paid journeys are yet to be granted, but may not be that far off.
Taken together, these developments indicate that AV regulation in the EU and UK is entering a more operational phase. Businesses across the AV supply chain should be engaging now to closely monitor the rules still being written and to prepare for the compliance obligations that are already or will shortly be in effect.

Accenture and osapiens have worked with DS Smith to help the company gain full transparency into the origin and movement of European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) relevant materials across its Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) supply chain.
The EUDR will come into force in December 2026 and aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss by boosting the consumption of ‘deforestation-free’ products and by reducing the EU’s impact on global deforestation and forest degradation.
The collaboration with Accenture and osapiens for improved supply chain governance and data management has helped establish a foundation for DS Smith to meet future sustainability and product compliance requirements.
Reportedly, the company can now trace EUDR-relevant materials throughout its EMEA supply chain, from origin through production and distribution, with clear, auditable proof of where the materials in the packaging come from. Suppliers are onboarded digitally, and traceability and compliance information is managed through a centralized system, providing greater visibility into supplier and material data.
Together, DS Smith, Accenture and osapiens reviewed sourcing, manufacturing, logistics and sales processes across more than 250 DS Smith plants and facilities in more than 30 countries. Accenture helped drive process transformation, supplier enablement, systems integration and program scaling, while osapiens provided the technology platform supporting the initiative. The companies then established a more consistent approach for managing DS Smith’s supplier and traceability data. Previously separate supply chain systems, onboarding and reporting processes were integrated into one single platform, the osapiens HUB.
“Nearly 80% of supply chain leaders tell us that uncertain geopolitical regulatory requirements have made operating their businesses more difficult over the past six months. That pressure is not going away,” said Matias Pollmann-Larsen, Global Risk, Resilience and Sustainable Value Chain lead, Accenture. “What DS Smith has done with Accenture and osapiens is build the data foundation needed to stay ahead of these challenges, rather than simply responding to the next regulation when it arrives.”
“For an organization operating across as many countries and facilities as DS Smith, having reliable, consistent data about your supply chain is not straightforward,” said Sakis Miliotis, IT director for Paper, Paper Supply Chain, Recycling and Sustainability, DS Smith. “Working with Accenture and osapiens, we have built something that works at scale. Our teams can now access the information they need, suppliers can submit data through a streamlined process, and we have a clear, auditable view of EUDR relevant materials from source to delivery. That gives us a strong foundation we can build on as compliance requirements evolve.”
“The challenge for most organizations is not a shortage of supply chain data, but rather that the data sits in too many places, in too many formats, with too many gaps,” said Stephan de Barse, chief revenue officer, osapiens. “This project shows what becomes possible when those challenges are addressed: with the osapiens HUB, more than 1,000 suppliers engaged through a single process, compliance managed proactively and reporting made significantly more efficient.”
In other news, DS Smith and Schneider Electric have teamed up on a fully recyclable corrugated cardboard solution for three integrated electrical switchgear products, aiming to reduce material use and improve supply chain circularity.
Elsewhere, the International Molded Fiber Association (IMFA) has launched a European Regulation Tracker to help its members understand and adjust to policy changes that could affect their access to the European market, all through a single platform.

articles.summary: EU turns page on Ukraine's $27bn deficit, says all needs are covered  Euronews.comUkraine’s war chest is running low at the worst possible moment  politico.euUkraine's 2026 budget, defence needs are covered, EU says  ReutersUkraine's finances: everything we don't know  The Kyiv IndependentEU Shuts Door to Early Loan Payout for Kyiv and Demands Reform  bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
The mystery surrounding Ukraine's $27 billion shortfall abruptly ended on Thursday as the European Commission confirmed the country's financial and military needs for 2026 are fully covered.
The European Commission has concluded that Ukraine's financial and military needs for this year are fully met, one month after Kyiv flagged a $27 billion (€23.92 billion) shortfall in its Ministry of Defence that caught Brussels off guard.
"Today, through coordinated joint efforts, we have identified the means to cover Ukraine's budget and defence needs for 2026," the Commission said in a vaguely worded statement shared by President Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday.
"We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release."
With this, the executive closes the debate that began in late August when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on allies to fill the $27 billion gap, warning essential weapon deliveries were at risk.
"We need more money, much more," Zelenskyy said.
Since then, the Commission has been engaged in technical talks with the Ukrainian government to pin down the exact scope of the financing hole.
From the outset, EU officials were reluctant to validate the $27 billion figure, later reduced to $20 billion, which they considered unexpected and unexplained.
Instead, they shifted the focus to the €90 billion loan, the bloc's main line of assistance. It foresees €45 billion for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027.
At first, Zelenskyy suggested that a share of the loan earmarked for next year be moved to this year, but the request was never formalised.
As technical talks dragged on, Brussels dialled up the pressure on Kyiv to advance the reforms necessary to unlock the support loan and the Ukraine Facility, a prior assistance envelope. The Commission is frustrated by the slow legislative pace.
The loan and the facility have roughly $37 billion still available until the end of the year, which EU officials insist is enough to keep Ukraine on a solid footing.
With 2026 settled, attention now turns to the much direr 2027.
In its statement, the Commission promised to "swiftly" allocate the loan's second €45 billion half to ensure fast disbursements, "subject to the established conditions".
Brussels and Kyiv will "begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs", it added, urging allied nations to increase their contributions.
"All sides agreed that other partners should also fulfil their financial commitments and step up their efforts in light of the significant challenges Ukraine is facing."
In response to the Commission's statement, Zelenskyy praised the "good results" of the bilateral consultations about the 2026 and 2027 needs.
"We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage," he said. "Going forward, we will coordinate this work and align our actions every month, ensuring continuous coordination."
Earlier this week, Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said the country faces a staggering $78 billion hole in 2027: $32.6 billion on the budget and $45 billion on military expenditures. (The Commission has not yet validated the numbers.)
Marchenko warned that Russia's non-stop attacks, targeting data centres, telecoms, power grids, factories and railways, coupled with the blockade in the Black Sea, threaten to paralyse the Ukrainian economy and cripple tax collection.
The wartime costs for 2027 could exceed Marchenko's estimates, says Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategy in Kyiv.
"These are the realities of war. When the €90 billion support loan was adopted, the partners understood that Ukraine would still need to seek additional resources to meet all its necessary needs. And we did indeed expect that part of the defence needs would be covered by in-kind support," Myronenko told Euronews.
"Unfortunately, that in-kind support has decreased, increasing the need for additional funding. Moreover, the war is indeed becoming more expensive and more intense."

Both Smith and Willis had overseen investigations into President Donald Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election.
But Schmitt’s allegation rested on an apparent mix-up between the Atlanta Hawks and the Iowa Hawkeyes during the hearing to the visible shock of onlookers.
Prior to the blunder, Schmitt had sought Justice Department material that might establish a link between the two investigations, sources told MS NOW. The request came amid a broader GOP effort to portray the criminal probes into Trump as highly coordinated witch hunts.
Schmitt was later given access to text messages related to Smith. But committee staff “explicitly warned Schmitt's team that the texts were unvetted and that it was their responsibility to verify the information,” the outlet reported.
What followed was an embarrassing moment, broadcast live to viewers across the country.
During his questioning, Schmitt said he had obtained text messages showing Smith attended a Hawks game in Atlanta on February 3, 2024. When Smith appeared confused and said he had not been at the game, Schmitt replied: “I think you’ve already perjured yourself.”
His aides then briefly held up a poster board that appeared to show text messages indicating seats had been reserved for Smith.
Schmitt concluded by calling Smith a “villain” and a “total dirtbag” who “weaponized the Department of Justice against political enemies to an extent that has never happened in the history of this country.”
Soon after, Smith suggested he understood the apparent mix-up. He said he had attended a women’s college basketball game in Maryland around the time frame Schmitt described — Iowa’s Hawkeyes playing the University of Maryland.
Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, also came to Smith’s defense, criticizing Schmitt for leveling accusations without first verifying the facts.
“That might be the confusion over the names of the team,” Klobuchar said. “But perhaps you should’ve looked at it more carefully.”
“I think that people should have their facts straight before they accuse someone of being a dirtbag and not get the teams wrong,” she added.
Schmitt later said he did not regret his questioning, telling Politico that Smith “has lied before to Congress.”
Smith’s two federal cases against Trump — one involving alleged election interference and the other classified documents — were dismissed after Trump won the 2024 election.
The Georgia case brought by Willis stalled after the Georgia Court of Appeals removed Willis from the prosecution in December 2024, citing the appearance of impropriety stemming from her relationship with a special prosecutor. A subsequent prosecutor ultimately declined to pursue the case.

articles.title: National authorities must work together to ensure consistent enforcement of EUDR - Oils & Fats International
articles.summary: National authorities must work together to ensure consistent enforcement of EUDR  Oils & Fats International
articles.full_text:
With the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) coming into force from 1 January, national authorities need to be aligned to prevent palm oil entering Europe through more lenient entry points, the OFI Commercial/Technical conference heard in Amsterdam last week.
The conference was one of four held under one roof from 21-23 September at the OFI International 2026 show, which attracted more than 350 people from over 30 countries.
“The EUDR is a welcome and loved baby but its delivery has been long and painful,” said Ruben Brunsveld, deputy director, market transformation EMEA, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO).
Originally due to take effect on 30 December 2024, the EUDR has been delayed twice but is now set to come into force for large- and medium-sized companies on 1 January, and for small and micro operators on 30 June 2027.
Companies placing palm oil, soya, cocoa, coffee, cattle, rubber or timber goods on the EU market will need to have a functioning due diligence system to prove these commodities are deforestation-free, legally produced and traceable to their source.
Brunsveld told the conference that while RSPO certification did not substitute an operator’s due diligence responsibilities, it could demonstrate compliance in required risk analysis, traceability and National Competent Authority (NCA) checks.
He identified three outstanding issues in the implementation of the EUDR – data sharing, the new Annex 1 to the EUDR, and different national approaches to implementation.
Data sharing: Under the EUDR, companies will need to submit due diligence statements (DDSs) into an EU information system, throwing up questions on who owns the data, who has access to it, and the protection of sensitive commercial information.
Annex 1: The July 2026 revision of Annex I - which determines which products fall within the EUDR - removed some products from scope and added others, including certain palm oil derivatives. The new products would become subject to the EUDR from 30 December 2027, and it remained to be seen how companies would respond to this, Ruben said.
National implementation: While the EUDR is an EU law, it is up to each country’s NCA to enforce it.
Ruben said NCAs needed to be aligned to prevent different entry points into Europe, especially if some NCAs were more lenient in enforcing the EUDR than others.
Marieke Leegwater, senior policy advisor at Solidaridad, added that there was increasing evidence that smallholders were being excluded from EU value chains because of lack of documentation and the complexities of organising data; and it was often unclear how farmer data ownership would be protected.
“For palm oil, smallholders are being pushed out of value chains to Europe. It started with the RSPO and the EUDR has made it worse.”
European palm oil volumes were now mostly supplied from bigger estates and a solution needed to be found to include smallholders, she said.
- EU-Indonesia palm oil trade
Relating to palm oil, Frans Claassen, managing director of MVO – the Netherlands oils and fats industry association – said the new the EU-Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) could make Indonesian palm oil significantly more attractive for the EU.
“CEPA will introduce annual duty and levy-free export quotas for Indonesian palm oil to the EU. The quota starts with 1.9M tonnes and increases by 3% for nine consecutive years.”
The agreement – set to come into force in early 2027 – would abolish current 3.8% EU import duties on crude palm oil (CPO); 12.8% duties on solid fractions (immediate packings, maximum 1kg); 10.9% of ‘other’ solid fractions; 5.1% duties on refined/bleach/deodorised (RBD) palm oil or palm olein for non-food applications; and 9% duties for ‘other’ RBD palm oil or palm olein.
Claassen explained that Indonesia accounted for a 10% share of total EU CPO imports of 1.68M tonnes in 2025, and a 51% share of the EU’s total processed palm oil imports of 1.46M tonnes that year, giving it a 29% share of total EU imports of palm oil.
At the Indonesian September 2026 palm oil reference price of US$1,007.51/tonne, CEPA would remove US$268.90/tonne in export duties and levies on CPO, and US$176.75/tonne of export duties and levies on RBD palm oil, which could make Indonesian CPO significantly more attractive for the EU.
However, the actual benefits fully depended on how Indonesia allocated the quotas, and European processors needed clarity on the practical operation and allocation of quotas “without delay”, Claassen said.
Dr Fadhil Hasan, senior economist and head of foreign affairs at the Indonesian Palm Oil Association (GAPKI), said that CEPA was in the process of ratification in Indonesia and would be passed in March.
On policy changes related to palm oil, Dr Hasan said the country’s new state-owned entity - Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI) – had been set up to improve governance in export activities and export earnings management, and to eliminate the risk of under-invoicing and transfer pricing.
“DSI is not the sole exporter of palm oil and other products.”
The government was also setting up a commodity exchange to make and strengthen palm oil price discovery.
And there was a shift in Indonesia’s mandatory biofuel blending programme to emphasise energy security, rather than as instrument to stabilise palm oil prices.
Dr Hasan added that due to strong El Niño effects this year, palm oil production would fall by 4-5M tonnes in 2027. Domestic consumption would increase by around 2M tonnes next year due to full B50 palm oil-based biodiesel mandatory blending, and exports would therefore decline next year.
Vegetable oil squeeze
Artem Hammerschmidt, head of vegetable oils and biofuels research at Cefetra Analytics, also spoke of a “major vegetable oil squeeze” in the next two years.
He said surging energy prices had strengthened the economic case for biofuels, raising the demand outlook for oils and fats.
In the USA, mandate-driven output requirements would rise by around 3M tonnes in 2026 and another 2M tonnes in 2027, forcing US biodiesel/HVO and SAF producers back into imported oils and fats. Indonesia’s palm oil use for biodiesel, driven by its B50 biodiesel mandate, was also set to lift domestic palm oil use for biodiesel to 16.8M tonnes, curtailing exports.
Hammerschmidt said total oils and fats requirements for FAME, HVO and SAF in 2025 totalled 58.9M tonnes but were forecast to jump by 6-7M tonnes in 2026 and by another 7M tonnes in 2027 to total 72.5M tonnes.
“The challenge is not absorbing one exceptional increase but doing so for two consecutive years.”
With El Niño setting the stage for a major vegetable oil squeeze, global production of oils and fats was expected to fall by 0.3M tonnes in 2026/27, exports could fall by 0.8M tonnes and stocks could plunge by 3.3M tonnes as demand jumped 5.7M tonnes, he said.
Limited global supply of used and waste oils also meant Europe would increasingly rely on rapeseed oil as a biofuel feedstock, with producers having to pay more for used cooking oil (UCO) as suppliers would need to go further afield to find and collect new supplies.
UCO
Because UCO is increasingly used as a raw material for biofuels, the EU was introducing new requirements for UCO imports, explained Steven Danneel, Coordinating Senior Inspector, Animal By-products, Tactical Direction & Expertise Division, Directorate Enforcement, of the Netherlands Food and Consumer Products Safety Authority (NVWA).
- Danneel told the OFI Commercial/Technical conference that UCO could originate from vegetable oils such as soyabean and palm oils, or animal-based sources such as tallow.
Under the new rules, due to come into force on 19 November 2027, UCO containing or consisting of animal-origin material would be considered as Category 3 material under the EU Animal By-products (ABP) regulation.
The imported ABP UCO had to originate from an ABP-approved or registered operator in the third country, which would be an issue, he said.
This was because UCO may be collected from many small sources; authorities in the exporting country would have to oversee the different operators and provide relevant information for EU purposes; and existing UCO supply chains may not be structured for this.
- Danneel added that as it was not always possible to test if UCO came from animal origins, traceability would need to be document-based, rather than from analysis of the product.
- The OFI Commercial/Technical Conference was organised by Oils & Fats International (OFI) and MVO - The Netherlands Oils and Fats Industry association.
- The conference and the OFI International 2026 show, held at the Amsterdam Congress Centre, was supported by the Netherlands Oils, Fats and Oilseeds Trade Association (NOFOTA) and FOSFA International. The event also featured a major exhibition of suppliers to the oils and fats industry and three other conferences organised by the German Society for Fat Science (DGF); Euro Fed Lipid (EFL) and Triact.

articles.title: France’s budget offers no quick relief for bond markets - ING Think
articles.summary: France’s budget offers no quick relief for bond markets  ING Think
articles.full_text:
France’s fiscal package would prevent the deficit from reaching 6.5% of GDP next year, but it would not stabilise public debt. With a difficult political process ahead, French bonds are likely to remain under pressure, while the threshold for ECB intervention remains high
What is in the new budget?
France’s minority government today presented its plans for the state budget (PLF), and a separate bill covering the financing of the social security system (PLFSS). The government aims to bring the public deficit back to 5% of GDP in 2027, after an expected increase from 5.1% in 2025 to 5.4% in 2026. Without corrective measures, the deficit would instead reach around 6.5% next year, as interest payments, pensions and other expenditure continue to rise.
The budget contains €43bn of measures compared with this no-policy-change scenario. Together with the growing impact of previous decisions, the total effort affecting the 2027 accounts would reach €54bn.
Much of the adjustment would come from higher revenues. The tax burden would rise from 43.9% to 44.2% of GDP through targeted measures affecting households and companies. These include a lower tax allowance for pensioners, changes to the taxation of sick leave and termination payments, fewer tax exemptions and stronger action against fraud. The surcharge on large companies would remain in place, while employers’ social security reductions would be cut.
Public spending would continue to rise, but more slowly than economic growth. It would decline only slightly as a share of GDP, from 57.1% in 2026 to 56.9% in 2027. Interest payments are projected to jump by €12bn to €91bn, while defence spending would rise by €6.4bn.
Savings would therefore fall on other areas. Most ministerial budgets and civil service pay would be frozen, along with housing benefits and family allowances. Higher pensions would not be indexed to inflation, generating €4.1bn in savings, while smaller pensions would be protected. Healthcare and local government spending would also be more tightly controlled. The structural effort (excluding cyclical factors and the debt burden) to reduce the deficit is estimated at 1.2% next year, which is in line with the European criteria limiting the growth of so-called ‘controllable’ expenditure (at +0.7 per cent, the lowest rate of growth since 2017).
Even if fully implemented, the budget would only slow the deterioration. Public debt, already at 119% of GDP in mid-2026, is projected to reach 121.7% in 2027. A deficit of 5% would still be far too high to stabilise it.
A modified budget is the most likely outcome
The two bills must be formally filed at the National Assembly by 6 October, with the plenary debate scheduled to begin on 13 October. From the filing date, parliament has 70 days to complete the procedure for the state budget and 50 days for the social security budget. The main deadlines will therefore fall between late November and mid-December.
A straightforward parliamentary agreement appears unlikely given the absence of a stable majority. The more plausible route is that several weeks of negotiations produce a modified budget, but not enough support for a formal vote. The government could then use Article 49.3 of the constitution, which allows it to pass the bill without a formal vote, unless an absolute majority of MPs vote to bring down the government.
A successful no-confidence motion would force the government to resign and prevent the budget from being adopted through Article 49.3. It would not automatically trigger a general election, which would require a separate decision by the president.
If parliament failed to complete the procedure before the constitutional deadlines, the government could try to implement the budget by ordinance. This has never been done for a budget under the Fifth Republic and would be politically and legally contentious. If no full budget were ready by 1 January, a special law could temporarily maintain existing taxes and essential expenditure, but that would lead to a sharper deterioration of public finances.
The key question therefore is whether the opposition can assemble an absolute majority for censure. Both the Socialist Party and the Rassemblement National face a difficult choice. Bringing down the government would underline their opposition, but could prolong the uncertainty and leave the winner of the 2027 presidential election facing an even more urgent fiscal problem.
The RN currently appears inclined to avoid censure. According to Le Monde, it would prefer to enter 2027 with an imperfect budget that could later be amended rather than inherit no full budget and have to prepare an emergency one after the election. Crucially, the RN and the Socialists do not need to support the budget. For them, it might look more comfortable to blame the current government for the austerity policies in the run-up to the presidential elections. Unless they unite behind the same no-confidence motion, the motion is unlikely to secure the required majority.
A modified budget is therefore likely to be adopted eventually, probably through Article 49.3 rather than a parliamentary vote. But before that, the coming weeks are likely to bring lengthy negotiations, amendments and shifting political positions.
Buying time, not solving the problem
Adopting a full budget would be a relative success. It would prevent the deficit from rising towards 6.5% and avoid a prolonged period without a proper fiscal framework.
But it would not resolve France’s structural fiscal problems. The deficit would remain too high to stabilise the debt ratio, while ageing-related expenditure and interest payments would continue to rise. The next government will therefore have to make further difficult choices.
So far, none of the main presidential candidates has presented a sufficiently detailed plan explaining which expenditure would be reduced, which taxes would change or how the debt ratio would eventually be stabilised. The 2027 budget could buy France some time. It would not make the fiscal problem disappear.
Charlotte de Montpellier
Bond spreads face further widening pressure as positive catalysts remain elusive
The budget plan marks a substantial effort towards fiscal consolidation. It may offer some temporary relief for spreads. But this is the government trying to convey the urgency of the situation – and bond markets will watch whether parliament takes notice or remains preoccupied with pre-election positioning.
Even taking into account some potential relief now, looking ahead we see spreads remaining in a range well above the 100bp level – more likely testing levels towards 150bp.
At the time of writing, the widely watched 10y OAT/bund spread has already topped 130bp. That is a 46bp widening since the start of September when the spread stood at 86bp. Picking out next target levels appears arbitrary at this point, as there are few anchors to hold on to. The next local highs were at 145bp, last seen during the sovereign debt crisis. The combination of increased volatility and a prolonged timeline of uncertainty is likely to keep the spread under widening pressure as it curbs investor appetite for French risk even if valuations start to look stretched. A positive catalyst appears elusive for now.
With a view to next year’s presidential elections, the candidates’ fiscal plans remain too vague to offer reassurance. With the latest polling results coming in, markets are increasingly concerned about the presidential race becoming a face-off between Le Pen on the far right and Melenchon on the far left. That is another potentially growing tail risk that markets have to consider, risking further spread widening. Remember that Melenchon spooked the establishment with a controversial proposal to convert French bonds held at the Bank de France into zero-coupon perpetual bonds.
There was a notable shift from the market pricing a mainly political risk premium towards pricing actual credit risk, at least judged by the credit default swaps market. French 5y CDS spreads have widened by 36bp to 72bp since the start of September. In terms of dynamics, it slightly surpassed the pandemic impact, and we are now on par with levels last seen when Le Pen ran on a ‘Frexit’platform in the 2017 elections.
It is important to add some perspective: the levels are only slightly above a range where Italy was traded from 2024 to early 2025 – and Italy’s spread had spiked to above 250bp when the pandemic hit. But before markets can return to assessing France’s pricing relative to underlying fundamentals, we will likely need to see political stability first. A path that Italy has also shown.
Benjamin Schröder
Will the ECB step in?
The widening French spread raises the question of whether the ECB could intervene through its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI). TPI allows the ECB to purchase securities issued by member states whose financing conditions have deteriorated for reasons not justified by country-specific fundamentals. However, before activating it, the Governing Council considers a cumulative set of criteria to determine whether the countries concerned are pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. In practice, this includes compliance with the EU fiscal framework, which would, at a minimum, require the proposed French budget to be fully adopted. Hence, the statement of Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin: “There are mechanisms that are linked to very critical situations on markets that prevent the proper transmission of monetary policy. But these mechanisms are only used if measures are taken at a national level.”
The ECB has nevertheless left itself some discretion, stating that the intervention criteria “will be dynamically adjusted to the unfolding risks and conditions to be addressed”. Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all the weapons at their disposal if the country is attacked by Europe in his latest sabre-rattling threat.
The Russian president reiterated Moscow's long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries, but said it would respond to any attacks with all its arsenal.

It comes as several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region”. They provided no evidence to support such a claim.
“There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate (the) Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday.

South Korean president Lee Jae Myung says Seoul will take additional measures if Ukraine continues to deny the existence of a confidentiality agreement related to the repatriation of North Korean prisoners of war, and called on Kyiv to acknowledge the agreement and apologise.
In a post on X, Lee also expressed grave regret over Ukraine's response, accusing Kyiv of undermining South Korea's head of state and warning that remarks about an imminent military clash between North and South Korea amounted to invoking the risk of war on the Korean Peninsula.
Russian air strikes hit Southern Bridge in Kyiv again, says mayor
Russian air strikes have again hit the Southern Bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Friday.
On Thursday, Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and into the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, triggering fires in the capital, as Moscow continues its near-daily around-the-clock strikes on Ukraine.

The 49-year-old American rapper was scheduled to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October.
Writing on the messaging platform Telegram, Moscow-based promoter Say Agency announced that the dates had been scrapped.

Russia has intensified airstrikes as its overall frontline advances have slowed this year.
One person was wounded on Thursday in a Russian attack on a business centre in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, regional officials said.
City administration chief Serhiy Lysak said infrastructure had been damaged but gave no further details.
Odesa and the surrounding region have been a frequent target of attacks aimed partly at choking Kyiv's export revenues.
Russia, which says it strikes only military targets, reported that it had attacked a data centre in Odesa and a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine has also stepped up attacks on Russia, striking oil refineries and major online retailers to try to undermine Moscow's war effort.
One man was killed when a Ukrainian drone exploded in the town of Graivoron in Russia's Belgorod region, local authorities said on Thursday.
Merz warns of more Russian hybrid attacks as he reaffirms support for Ukraine
Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Thursday that Germany faced more hybrid attacks from Russia as he pledged to continue support for Ukraine ahead of what is likely to be its harshest winter since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022.
German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber attacks, accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
"We are preparing for further hybrid attacks, including serious ones," Merz said in a speech marking the award of the 2026 Westphalian Peace Prize to the NATO alliance.
Moscow has rejected the accusations from Western governments and intelligence services.Speaking to a forum of Russia experts on Thursday, President Vladimir Putin said Moscow was not about to attack foreign factories that produce weapons for Ukraine but that this was something Russian intelligence services needed to track closely.
Merz and his conservatives have been badly weakened by elections in two eastern German states last month in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) triumphed.

articles.title: Bull doubles supercomputer output in France to feed Europe’s AI push - Crypto Briefing
articles.summary: Bull doubles supercomputer output in France to feed Europe’s AI push  Crypto Briefing
articles.full_text:
The newly state-owned French manufacturer has expanded its Angers factory to 12 racks a month as EuroHPC orders pile up
Europe wants its own AI infrastructure. Somebody has to bolt it together, and in France that job increasingly falls to Bull SAS.
On October 1, 2026, the state-owned supercomputer maker inaugurated an expanded factory in Angers. The upgrade doubles monthly production capacity from 6 racks to 12. That makes it one of the clearest physical signs yet that the continent’s push for computing sovereignty is moving beyond policy papers.
Inside the Angers expansion
The expansion cost €80 million. It is a direct response to rising European demand for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems.
There may be more headroom still. The factory has the potential to scale to 24 racks per month by 2027, though that remains a possibility rather than a commitment.
The extra floor space has a practical payoff. Bull can now build major systems side by side instead of queuing them one after another. Two flagship projects are currently moving through the plant in parallel.
The first is Alice Recoque, a 94-rack supercomputer. The second is LUMI-AI, a system destined for Finland and valued at €388 million. LUMI-AI is the largest contract in Bull’s history. It also marks the sixth AI Factory under the EuroHPC program, the EU’s joint initiative for building shared supercomputing infrastructure.
At the old capacity of 6 racks a month, Alice Recoque alone would have occupied the line for more than a year.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
A record year for orders
The capacity bump is not speculative. CEO Emmanuel Le Roux reported record order intake for Bull in 2026.
The company won 15 of 18 EuroHPC tenders this year.
Commercial demand is growing too. Bull signed a deal worth nearly €100 million with Airbus to expand the aerospace giant’s simulation capabilities.
From Atos spinoff to state asset
Bull’s current shape is quite new. The company became 100% state-owned on March 31, 2026, after the French state bought it from Atos for up to €404 million.
The broader policy backdrop is the EU’s €7 billion investment plan covering 2021 to 2027. The goal is a pan-European supercomputing network that narrows the technology gap with the United States and China.
Bull’s systems now contain approximately 70% European component content. Five years ago, that figure stood at 20-30%.
The accelerator problem
There is a notable asterisk on the sovereignty story. The most important chips inside these machines still come from America.
Bull’s accelerators are predominantly sourced from AMD. Some configurations use Nvidia or Intel instead.
Bull is also working on the assembly side of that equation. A partnership with Foxconn allows certain Nvidia NVL systems to be assembled in Europe.

When searching for animals to aid their operations, most militaries and national guards opt for German Shepherds and other large pooches.
But Mexico’s National Guard have chosen an 8-inch-tall, 15-pound kitted-out Chihuahua named Comando.
The small dog was adopted around six months ago while still a puppy after his elderly owners were unable to continue caring for him.
Now, Comando is training to assist with search-and-rescue work while also serving as an unofficial mascot for the National Guard.
He has his own fitted vest, miniature goggles and a head-mounted camera to assist in his very important work.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
He’s also shown bravery already – during a training session, Comando jumped into action and passed an obstacle course while a fully trained larger dog sat frozen.
Lieutenant Debora Hernandez said that Comando is reminding many that ‘beneath the uniform, we are human beings.’
Though his role (and size) is small, his service is sure to aid the National Guard as it continues to fight against organised crime in the country.
Cartels are dotted across Mexico, and have been fighting turf wars and for control of drug supply from Sinaloa to the Gulf for decades.
Earlier this year, an influx of violence across Mexico after the death of drug lord ‘El Mencho’ brought cartels back into the global spotlight.
Forced disappearances, murders in broad daylight and mass graves have become common as the cartels fight to defend their ‘turf’ and protect drug supplies.
