Russia is planning to boost military spending by 27%, it has been reported, amid rumours of further mobilisation and warnings of increased ‘hybrid’ attacks in Europe.
Vladimir Putin proposes to spend 17.1 trillion roubles (£154billion) on defence in 2027, according to government documents seen by the Reuters news agency.
That is a rise of more than a quarter on the 13.5 trillion roubles (£122billion) originally budgeted.
The document states that defence spending in the next three years will total 50 trillion roubles (£450billion).
Putin’s commitment to war comes after UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting labelled Russia the biggest threat to the country’s security.
‘We’ve got war in our continent. We’ve got a Russian president who has imperialist ambitions, who is constantly testing Britain’s defences, Nato defences and testing the strength of our alliances,’ he said last weekend.

‘And so, the sobering reality is that we face a greater risk of war than we’ve done at any point in my lifetime.’
Speaking today, Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia is ‘testing us across Europe’, describing ‘airspace violations, arson, sabotage, and of course, the Russian hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in August’.
‘But while we see no imminent military attack against Nato, we must be prepared for Russia’s campaign of hostile actions against allies to continue,’ he added.
‘We must all remain vigilant.’
Russia has warned Nato it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance moved to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave bordering the Baltic Sea.
In a document seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a ‘dangerous and reckless course’ that entailed ‘high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict’.
The document said this included the possibility of ‘Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance’s member states right from the outset’.
‘Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,’ the diplomatic note said.
The warning highlighted Moscow’s urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing Nato threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarised Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova cited statements by dignitaries from Nato states which she said demonstrated ‘Russophobia’ and a readiness to wage war with Moscow.
These figures, Zakharova wrote, ‘need to be brought back down to earth. We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed.’ ‘If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different sort of war – a very short war,’ she added.
Nato spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed on Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the US-led military alliance.
‘We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,’ she said in a statement.
Hart insisted that Nato is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply, ‘noting that Nato is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia’.
Kaliningrad is surrounded by Nato members Poland and Lithuania.
It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets.
Nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there.
Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever launch an attack on any Nato ally.
Nato allies have conducted a series of military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months.
More are planned in October.
It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines.

The UK needs to be prepared for financial market shocks as a result of artificial intelligence (AI) and must ensure the system is “resilient”, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.
Andrew Bailey cautioned that “not everybody always wins” when questioned about the hundreds of billions currently being invested in the AI sector, and warned that the technology could be a “potentially very powerful weapon” in the wrong hands.
Asked what the risks and benefits could be to the UK, Mr Bailey said it had “great potential to strengthen growth in our economies”, as the market values some AI firms as multi-trillion pound businesses.
AI chipmaker Nvidia currently has a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn) due to enormous investments by those who believe in the future of the technology, while tech giants such as Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are investing significant funds to develop their own models.
Two of the largest AI companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, are also preparing to float shares on the US stock markets, in a move likely to raise them hundreds of billions of dollars more in investments.
Just this week, OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman delayed the launch of the company’s latest model due to safety issues that had occurred during internal testing. The firm has faced intense scrutiny since July, after its AI agent hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face without being prompted, and accessed non-public information within the Australian government.
The company is likely to be listed on the stock market in 2027, with Mr Altman reiterating his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".
Mr Bailey told the BBC that AI has created a "much more powerful way of uncovering vulnerabilities".
"It's revealing things that have been in bits of operating software that we've had, and all of us have had."
"In the wrong hands... it's a very powerful, potentially very powerful, weapon," he added.
Mr Bailey himself was the subject of recent deepfake images created by AI, which depicted him and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage engaging in a fist fight.
He said the bank had struggled to find the origin of the images, which circulated on X.
He continued: "There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth.
"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."
"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".
"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.
"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

articles.full_text:
Sanofi is paying Regeneron $1 billion upfront to collaborate on four early-stage immunology programs, teeing the longstanding partners up to try to replicate Dupixent’s success.
Dupixent, an antibody that targets IL-4 and IL-13, generated 5.2 billion euros ($5.9 billion) for Sanofi in the second quarter and is the cornerstone of the French pharma's business. With the U.S. patent on the compound expiring in 2031—and Sanofi’s efforts to develop new growth drivers stuttering—the Paris-based drugmaker has looked for next-generation assets under new CEO Belén Garijo, M.D., Ph.D.
The search led Sanofi back to Regeneron’s door. Sanofi is paying the blockbuster upfront fee and pledging up to $7 billion in milestones to split the costs and profits for four assets in development at Regeneron. In a statement, Garijo called the deal “a deliberate first step in igniting Sanofi’s innovation engine.”
REGN20423, a long-acting IL-13 monoclonal antibody, is the most advanced of the four assets covered by the deal. Regeneron began a first-in-human trial in May to test the drug candidate in healthy volunteers and eczema patients.
The three preclinical assets target IL-4 and IL-4 receptor alpha, including an IL-4xIL-13 bispecific. Regeneron aims to start clinical trials of the drug candidates next year. The U.S. biopharma has an option to add lunsekimig, a Sanofi asset targeting TSLP and IL-13, to the collaboration after seeing phase 3 data in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Regeneron will lead R&D for its four assets, and Sanofi will lead global commercialization. The agreement marks a new phase in an alliance that has been hugely successful but, in recent years, somewhat fraught. Regeneron sued Sanofi in 2024, alleging its partner violated the terms of the Dupixent collaboration by refusing to share certain commercialization details.
Sanofi and Regeneron revealed in July that they were in talks about a new partnership. On an earnings call, Garijo said her main objective for the Regeneron relationship was “to rebuild trust.” The efforts have led to the deal and the settlement of the litigation.
The Sanofi deal coincided with Regeneron updates at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) conference. Adding Regeneron’s trevogrumab to semaglutide preserved over 70% of muscle mass loss compared to Novo’s GLP-1 drug at Week 52 of a clinical trial, Reuters reported.
Regeneron’s muscle data are part of an attempt to position trevogrumab in a congested market. At an EASD event hosted by Regeneron, presenters “argued that waist-to-height ratio may be more informative than BMI and emphasized the importance of adiposity, body composition and the quality of weight loss rather than weight reduction alone,” BMO Capital Markets analysts said in a note to investors.

articles.summary: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row  BBCRow between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs  Al JazeeraSouth Korea demands apology from Ukraine over disclosure of North Korean POW transfer  CNNWhy is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?  The GuardianUkrainian minister hopes to heal 'misunderstanding' with South Korea, media reports  Reuters
articles.full_text:
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.
Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.
Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".
Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.
Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".
"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.
Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".
"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

Three vessels reported being struck on Tuesday, September 29, in the area around the Strait of Hormuz as Iran appears to be lashing out to demonstrate that it is still threatening vessels. While it brings the total number of vessels struck to four so far this week, observers point to increasing oil flows and vessel traffic in the region.
UK Maritime Trade Operations reported the incidents, although few details were provided. It said that the information had come from verified sources but was delayed in being transmitted. It was unclear when the strikes took place. It identified all three incidents as involving tankers without details on the extent of the damage, while an unconfirmed report said one of the vessels was an LNG carrier.
Two of the vessels were identified in the tracking by the International Maritime Organization, with both being crude oil tankers flying the Liberian flag and sustaining damage. One VLCC, the Mersin Prosperity (299,319 dwt), is operated by ADNOC. The other tanker appeared to be a smaller vessel, possibly involved in the shuttle operations that have arisen to get oil from the Gulf states to tankers waiting south of the Strait in the Arabian Sea. This tanker was identified as Sinbad (115,949 dwt), and it was last reported at Fujairah. Both tankers appeared to be making the transit dark.
Iran’s Fars News Agency reported that warning shots were fired on Tuesday at vessels violating the Strait of Hormuz. It did not provide details on the incidents but said they accounted for the reports of explosions near Qeshm Island and other points along the coast. At the same time, an IRGC spokesperson, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, repeated the refrain that Iran controls the Strait. The Wana News Agency quotes him saying vessels attempting to transit the Strait without permission either will be targeted or will hit a mine.
Iran continues to make these claims while evidence builds that oil volumes are rising from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Iraq.
“Windward MIOC assesses that Iran is less able to constrain southern-corridor traffic than it was in mid-summer, as rising crude flows continue despite the threat to individual vessels,” writes Windward’s Zane Amundsen, MIOC Middle East Desk Lead. He cites 55 AIS-visible transits from September 16 to 23, while also concluding “the true number of transits is almost certainly higher.”
Most tankers are sailing with their AIS switched off. Windward also notes an increase in pipeline volume while saying transits are happening in the southern corridor, which remains under US CENTCOM air defense and naval support.
Tracking data from Windward shows 17 vessels transited Hormuz on September 29, after 16 vessels the prior day. It notes that roughly two-thirds of the oil volume, however, is moved through ship-to-ship transfers.
Kpler also notes that more than 70 percent of the crude that crossed the Strait of Hormuz in August changed tankers offshore. However, it reports that volumes excluding Iran returned to pre-war levels. It reports that in September volumes reached at least 16.5 mbd.

Oil volumes in part rebounded not by tanker but by the use of pipelines. Kpler assesses that around 40 percent of crude now leaves without crossing Hormuz, up from 17 percent before the war. It says that Saudi Arabia and the UAE are making greater use of pipeline routes for exports.
Saudi Arabia's pipeline route to the west and the terminal at Yanbu appear to have been restored after the previous attack by the Houthis. Windward reports that two VLCCs and two Suezmax tankers were loading a total of 6.2 million barrels at Yanbu on September 28, based on Vortexa data, after noting that all seven Yanbu crude berths were occupied on September 27. It notes that this was among the first cargoes leaving Yanbu since the September 10 attack, but that volume is only about two-thirds of the pre-attack pace.

articles.summary: Paramount-WBD Merger Is A Go As Judge Approves Legal Settlement, Last Hurdle To Close  DeadlineMark Ruffalo blasts Paramount-Warner Bros. merger after judge clears $110B Hollywood deal  Fox BusinessParamount-Warner Bros. Merger Set to Close Next Week After Judge OKs Settlement With State AGs  VarietyParamount gets court green light on Warner Bros deal, names Mattel's Kreiz co-CEO  ReutersUS judge approves settlement allowing Paramount to acquire Warner Bro...
articles.full_text:
UPDATED with CA AG statement, Block The Merger response: A federal judge has approved the Sept. 21 settlement between Paramount and a group of state Attorneys General that sued to block its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, removing the last hurdle for the deal to close.
“The Court finds the proposed consent decree represents a reasonable factual and legal resolution of the dispute,” wrote U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín today in her long awaited sign-off. “The parties’ proposed consent decree falls within the scope of the case made by the pleadings.”
Addressing critics of the September 21-unveiled settlement between the blue state AGs and ParaBros, the judge bluntly says: “The Court recognizes that this proposed consent decree reflects a compromise of the claims short of full adjudication – compromise that may leave some dissatisfaction for both sides and the public but a compromise that saves the risk, time, and expense of litigating through trial.”
Martínez-Olguín did not greenlight the settlement immediately, but allowed more than a week for opposition briefs to be filed, setting a Sept. 28 noon PT deadline for Paramount and the AGs to respond. It’s been a bit of a nail-biter as both sides awaited her final sign-off. Read her full order here.
Paramount CEO David Ellison said last week it would take about two weeks to formally combine the companies. That would bring it into next week. The faster the better for Paramount since it starts to rack up a so-called ticking fee to WBD shareholders of about $7 million a day starting Oct. 1 if the deal is not closed.
Twelve AGs led by Rob Bonta of California had been moving the antitrust trust case forward with a trial date set for March before the sides came together rather suddenly over the course of a few days. Bonta presented the agreement at a press conference with little enthusiasm, outlining the proposed remedies while insisting the agreement “is not a blessing” of the mega-deal and he still doesn’t think two of Hollywood’s biggest players should merge.
Today the much-criticised Bonta said, “We are pleased the court has approved our settlement. Our settlement with Paramount resolves our antitrust concerns in every market we brought in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and centers the needs, concerns, and futures of California workers.”
Having failed in its 11th-hour attempt at slow-walking Judge Martínez-Olguín’s approval of the settlement, Block the Merger Wednesday said, “In years to come, we’ll be able to point to this failure to put consumers over the monied interests of corporate consolidation as the tipping-point moment for media in this country. Allowing the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger to move forward with no meaningful structural remedies will cost jobs, mute creativity, weaken independent journalism, and damage our First Amendment rights. The ripples of this merger will be far-reaching, long-lasting, and impossible to contain.”
It’s been a long road. Paramount announced the deal in February after a string of hostile offers that WBD rejected. Adding sweeteners, Ellison eventually convinced the Warner board to agree to a combination, derailing a WBD-Netflix deal. It began moving briskly towards close until the AGs sued in July and the judge allowed the case to proceed. Paramount agreed to not close the deal while the suit was pending.
Attempted settlement talks stalled as Bonta and the AGs sought structural remedies like asset sales to address alleged antitrust violations in three markets: cable programming, wide-release movies and blockbuster films, the crux of the suit. Ellison demurred, but the sides ultimately came together and discussions accelerated.
There’s been significant opposition to the deal from the start, but also tremendous pressure on Bonta to put the case to rest as Ellison threatened to move the studio out of California.
In anticipation of the close, Paramount started marketing a $44 billion bond offering this week. Proceeds of the debt sale will fund the $110 billion acquisition, along with equity financing. With the coast now clear, the company will move quickly to close the complex transaction that will see it cash out WBD stockholders for $31 a share.
In the first major shakeup of the new regime, Cindy Holland, chair of Paramount’s Direct-to-Consumer business, has departed. Her last day was Tuesday, she said in a company memo. That leaves Casey Bloys, chairman-CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content, as the presumed streaming head of the combined Paramount-WBD.
A second shoe dropped this morning when Mattel chairman-CEO Ynon Kreiz stepped down rather abruptly. Shortly after Martínez-Olguín approved the settlement, Paramount announced Kreiz had been named co-CEO with Ellison.
The settlement includes a number of legally enforceable commitments by Paramount over five years following the close, like a set number of theatrical releases, an editorial oversight board for CNN and CBS, and negotiating separately with distributors for Paramount and WBD cable networks. There are some loopholes and there were no structural remedies. Read the settlement document here.
Continuing to address critics of the settlement who filed amicus briefs and wrote letters to the court, the judge noted their “dismay at many of the proposed consent decree’s provisions. However, a proposed consent decree like this one represents a negotiated settlement that does not fully remediate an alleged violation or even necessarily resolve the ultimate factual and legal issues of a case.”
She said “these hopes and desires for the proposed consent decree to reach farther – to achieve more – do not rise to the level of legal violations upon which the Court can reject the parties’ negotiated resolution.”

A proposal dated 16 September suggests a relationship between Canada and the European Union that would extend beyond trade, though any associate status would need to be negotiated from the ground up. Such a status would not automatically confer EU citizenship, free movement rights, a commissioner post, or voting rights in the European Council or the European Parliament.
Canada already has several building blocks in place. Trade data underscores the stakes. Any association agreement would require unanimity among the 27 member states as well as the European Parliament's consent. articles.title: Against the Tide, Autonomous Systems and Military AI Will Remain Under Human Control in Europe - Meta-Defense
articles.summary: Against the Tide, Autonomous Systems and Military AI Will Remain Under Human Control in Europe  Meta-Defense
articles.full_text:
On 9 April 2026, the German Federal Ministry of Defence set out the conditions for the use of artificial intelligence within the Bundeswehr. Regulation K-9000/102 keeps human beings at the centre of critical decisions, notably when they may lead to the use of force. This choice, aligned with European positions, comes at a time when the United States, Russia and China are accelerating the development of autonomous systems capable of detecting, coordinating and engaging targets with reduced, or even no, human intervention.
Table of contents
In Germany, Regulation K-9000/102 imposes human control and traceability on military AI and autonomous systems
Applicable to the development, testing, introduction and use of AI, the German text requires robust systems that are regularly tested and validated. Their operation must be subject to continuous monitoring, while data, outputs and responsibilities must remain traceable. These checks must continue after entry into service whenever risks, vulnerabilities or unforeseen effects require it, with the possibility of adapting or retraining the models concerned.
Personnel regularly using these tools must be able to verify the plausibility of their outputs and identify an erroneous recommendation before it is incorporated into a decision. The ministry therefore regards AI as an aid rather than an autonomous decision-maker. Responsibility for development, use and results remains assigned to identified individuals, including when the system is involved in a chain of command or in the selection and engagement of a military objective.
Each human check added to the chain linking a sensor, a headquarters and an effector nevertheless lengthens the decision loop. Several successive assessments can considerably reduce the responsiveness gained through automated data processing, particularly when timeframes are measured in seconds or milliseconds. An opposing force that authorises its systems to recognise a threat, allocate tasks and trigger an action without further human validation can then complete its cycle before the German decision has passed through all the prescribed checks.

articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON: The United States on Thursday announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran's largest automakers, as well as major rail, manufacturing and metals companies, as Washington seeks to exert maximum pressure in its war against the country.
"Because the rail and automotive sectors represent some of the regime's largest remaining sources of revenue and logistical capacity, today's action strikes directly at the critical arteries Iran relies on to sustain its economy and evade sanctions," the US Treasury said in a statement.
The new sanctions target the country's two largest automakers Iran Khodro (IKCO) and SAIPA, which service both the domestic market and export to regional trading partners.
In total, seven automakers were sanctioned under the new action, part of Washington's so-called "Operation Economic Outcast" launched as part of its drive to starve the Iranian government of revenue sources.
Niroo Motor, Iran's largest motorcycle manufacturer, was among those sanctioned.
Thursday's actions also took aim at international partners of Iran's auto sector, including Indonesia's Golden Motorcycle Company, and auto parts companies in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong.
Key Iranian rail companies sanctioned on Thursday include the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company (RAI), the Raja Passenger Trains Company and private freight carrier Sherkat-E Rah Ahan-E Khamle-O-Naghle.
The fresh sanctions also targeted major steel and other manufacturers in Iran, including Heavy Equipment Production Company (HEPCO), described by the US Treasury as "one of the Middle East's largest manufacturers of mining and road construction machinery."
Washington also sanctioned HEPCO's Shanghai-based subsidiary.
The new sanctions also targeted companies in the United Arab Emirates and Germany accused of aiding Iranian steel companies.
Finally, the new measures also targeted what was described as a complex steel and oil export network run by two Hong Kong-based Iranian-Dominican nationals.

A deal to sell one of the country's biggest shopping centres to a real estate giant for £516m has been agreed.
Landsec said it would launch a £500m equity fundraiser to help fund a deal to buy the Metrocentre in Gateshead, which attracts more than 16 million visitors each year, on Thursday.

Landsec previously said it planned to invest a further £1bn in major retail assets as part of its strategy.

articles.title: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners? - Yahoo News Australia
articles.summary: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners?  Yahoo News Australia
articles.full_text:
With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.
Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.
A trade order under strain
The EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.
Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."
Related
The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.
But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."
The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.
What each side wants
For the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence.
"We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.
For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.
Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.
The rule-taker question
The hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.
Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.
Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.
Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.
Related
Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.
The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.
Limits and risks
The idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.
Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.
Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

articles.title: Inflation accelerates in the eurozone, risk of more expensive loans grows - vijesti.me
articles.summary: Inflation accelerates in the eurozone, risk of more expensive loans grows  vijesti.me
articles.full_text:
Rising gas, petrol and diesel prices increase pressure on ECB to further raise interest rates
Inflation rose significantly faster than expected this month in some of the eurozone's largest economies due to an energy shock caused by the Iran war, increasing pressure on the European Central Bank to raise interest rates again.
The ECB has already raised interest rates twice this year to prevent the trend of rapid price increases from stabilizing, while investors have significantly increased expectations of further interest rate increases in recent weeks, as the prices of natural gas, gasoline and diesel have risen drastically.
Increasing interest rates would further complicate economic conditions and increase the cost of borrowing for states at a time when governments are already facing the highest yields on government bonds since the 2012 debt crisis, writes "Politiko".
In France, the harmonized inflation rate was 3,4 percent year-on-year in September, after 2,6 percent in August, while in Italy it jumped to 4,1 percent from 3,2 percent in August, data released yesterday showed. Both rates are well above the ECB's 2 percent target.
Inflation in Germany accelerated slightly more than expected, to 3,3 percent annually in September, up from 2,9 percent a month earlier. That is the highest inflation in Germany in almost three years, according to Reuters.
Core inflation, which excludes variable energy and food prices, remained unchanged for the third month in a row, at 2,4 percent.
In Spain, inflation rose to five percent in September, from 4,6 percent in August, data showed.
Energy price inflation appears to have exceeded expectations in all countries that have published data so far, while food price growth has also been somewhat higher, although much more moderate, JP Morgan's Mariana Monteiro told Reuters.
The national data comes ahead of eurozone-wide inflation data due on Friday. Economists interviewed by Reuters estimate that inflation in the bloc rose to 3,6 percent in September, up from 3,2 percent the previous month.
The ECB had expected inflation to rise from 3,3 percent in the third quarter to 3,6 percent in the last three months of the year, but economists believe the actual peak is likely to be closer to four percent, due to exceptionally high energy prices.
Markets are therefore now expecting four more interest rate hikes over the next year, on top of the two increases already implemented this summer.
"With little sign that tensions in the Middle East will ease any time soon and winter approaching, it is unlikely that energy prices will fall anytime soon," Rory Fensey, senior European economist at Oxford Economics, told the British agency.
According to the ECB's "adverse" scenario, inflation would be four percent in both the fourth quarter of this year and the first three months of 2027, and economists say current energy prices are close to that scenario.
In addition, the recent strengthening of the dollar will further aggravate Europe's inflation problems, as key raw materials are calculated in dollars, and the unfavorable exchange rate further increases the price of energy in local currencies.
Since this year's rise in inflation has not yet caused dangerous second-round effects across the eurozone, the European Central Bank's moderate monetary policy response remains appropriate, ECB President Christine Lagarde said on Monday.
Although the indirect effects of higher energy prices are starting to trickle down to other prices, it is unlikely to be enough to shift the balance in the ECB's decision-making, said Jack Allen-Reynolds, chief eurozone economist at Kapital Economics.
Core inflation has not risen significantly yet this year, but a new spike in energy prices means it could accelerate in early 2027, Fensi warned.

Households across the UK face new tax rules from today under changes announced by both new prime minister Andy Burnham and the previous government.
In a bid to tackle rising energy costs, VAT will be removed from household electricity bills from 1 October. The removal of the 5 per cent levy will save the average bill payer around £45 a year, estimates from the government show.
The policy was one of Mr Burnham’s first moves as prime minister, announced in July on the day after he took over the post.
Under current rules, energy providers currently charge the VAT rate on top of the amount of electricity used and the unit rate. Once this has been scrapped, they are expected to pass on the savings to households in full.
The cut will take effect on the same day that Ofgem’s energy price cap increases. The figure dictates the maximum unit price that providers can charge to households on a non-capped rate, which includes most households.
For October to the end of December, the price cap will rise to £1,723, an increase of £60 a year. Ofgem’s headline figure represents the annual bill for an average home, not the maximum that can be charged to a household.
The energy regulator will announce its next price cap, covering January to March 2027, in November. Experts have forecast a major rise, with large provider EDF now predicting a 30 per cent rise, to £2,098 – up £375 on October’s rate.
The stark forecasts come amid the US-Iran conflict, which have driven up energy costs worldwide. The effective seizure of the Strait of Hormuz – a major oil shipping lane – has seen the price of fuel and electricity spike at a rate last seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
In light of the continued conflict, the government is reportedly considering mirroring its electricity VAT policy to gas bills, which could take another £40 off energy bills on average. Any such change would now likely be announced at John Healey’s first Budget as chancellor at the end of October.
Another October change – tobacco and vapes
Also starting on 1 October is the increase to the amount of tax that is paid on both tobacco and vaping products.
From this date, there will be a new duty of £2.20 per 10ml on vaping products, which will apply whether they include nicotine or not. This means a £4 bottle containing 10ml vaping liquid will rise to £6.64, after VAT.
At the same time, cigarettes will also get more expensive. The existing tobacco duty will go up by an extra £2.20 per 100 cigarettes – meaning an extra 44p on a pack of 20 – and £2.20 per 50g of rolling tobacco.
The government says it has decided to increase both so that the cost of smoking cigarettes remains substantially higher than vaping, meaning consumers are more likely to choose to vape products over cigarettes.

President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Locked in a war in Ukraine which he said Russia had no choice but to launch in order to safeguard its own security, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westerly territory — Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania — was threatened.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
"This is inevitable," he said.
Putin said Russia realized it would be facing "an enemy [NATO] twice our size."
"And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers — we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it," he said. "But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage."
Nuclear warning
Putin's comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia's Baltic exclave.
Russia's warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is slightly bigger than the U.S. state of Connecticut. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by emphasising that it was a defensive alliance and that nuclear threats were not helpful.
Relations, already dire since Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.
"We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return," he said.
"At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state," Putin said.
"Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome," he added.
Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was worked out first, ruled out the idea of stopping Russian strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea area, while conceding that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.
But while he cast Western help to Kyiv when it came to launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack arms factories in Europe which supplied Ukraine "tomorrow."

The arrangement links continued production to changing Army budgets and Foreign Military Sales demand. It is intended to shorten the path from an allied purchasing decision to delivery while avoiding a production interruption across Sikorsky’s 230-supplier network.
Sikorsky Vice President and General Manager Rich Benton said the agreement accommodates changes in annual requirements. “We’ve come to this structure to give the Army flexibility as their needs and budget change year-to-year, while maintaining a vehicle that can support FMS demand.”
The company expects the structure to support allied orders as individual sales cases mature. “This agreement turns a partner‑nation decision into aircraft on the ramp faster than conventional procurement allows,” Benton said.
The award came ahead of a previously published year-end objective. Lockheed Martin said it sustains manufacturing at Sikorsky and its suppliers across 43 states.
The initial 16 helicopters will be funded through congressional appropriations for fiscal years 2025 and 2026 and proceeds from the Black Hawk Exchange and Sales Transaction program. That program allows the Army to reinvest revenue from sales of older aircraft in new helicopters.
“This contract ensures we maintain a ready, modern and survivable rotary‑wing capability for the Army and our allies,” said Col. Ryan Nesrsta, project manager for the Utility Helicopters Project Office. “The Black Hawk has long been a vital part of the Army and National Guard’s flexibility and will continue to be so for the next half century.”
The procurement agreement accompanies a broader effort to expand the Black Hawk’s capabilities. Sikorsky is implementing a higher-horsepower engine and airframe enhancements intended to increase payload capacity and extend range.

More than 5,000 Black Hawks have been delivered to more than 36 allied nations, according to the company. The helicopters have logged over 15 million flight hours, including approximately 5 million combat hours, supporting air assault, medical evacuation, disaster response and border security missions.
The Black Hawk industrial base supports approximately 55,000 U.S. jobs, with Sikorsky spending more than $1.5 billion annually. Lockheed Martin has also invested more than $1 billion over the past 11 years in Sikorsky plants and research laboratories in Connecticut, Alabama, Florida and New York.
“The people who manufacture Black Hawk helicopters, including 230 suppliers, hold skills that take years to develop and are hard to rebuild,” said Ken Demaree, vice president, Army and Air Force Systems at Sikorsky. “This agreement means the Army and our allies have aircraft coming without a pause in production.”

articles.title: Japan: competition policy and enforcement trends in digital markets and the rise of platform accountability - Global Competition Review
articles.summary: Japan: competition policy and enforcement trends in digital markets and the rise of platform accountability  Global Competition Review
articles.full_text:
This is an Insight article, written by a selected contributor as part of GCR's co-published content. Learn more about Insight
Introduction
This article provides an overview of the regulatory framework governing digital markets in Japan from the perspective of competition policy.
In recent years, Japan has actively enforced existing legislation – most notably the Antimonopoly Act (AMA), which serves as the foundation of its competition law regime – while also introducing new laws that either supplement or build upon the AMA.
Enforcement of existing laws has not been limited to orthodox measures such as cease-and-desist orders against AMA violations; it has also increasingly involved the use of commitment procedures –introduced at the end of 2018 – that enable case resolution without a formal finding of an AMA infringement. In addition, the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) has actively engaged in “advocacy” activities, raising social awareness of AMA compliance without specific enforcement through market surveys and the publication of reports.
Although law enforcement by competition authorities has traditionally played a prominent role in Japan, recent court decisions arising from private disputes concerning the interpretation of the AMA – such as the judgments of the District Court and High Court in the Tabelog case – have attracted significant attention.
Turning to legislative developments, new laws such as the Act on Improving Transparency and Fairness of Specified Digital Platforms (TFDPA) and the Act on Promotion of Competition for Specified Smartphone Software (also known as the Mobile Software Competition Act (MSCA)) were enacted on the basis of market studies and deliberations conducted either by the JFTC independently, or by the Digital Market Competition Headquarters, a body within the Cabinet Office comprising: the JFTC; the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI); the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC); and other relevant ministries.[1],[2]These agencies continue to collaborate in implementing the new regulatory regimes.
Legislative framework governing digital markets in Japan from the perspective of competition policy
Antimonopoly Act
Special legislation relating to digital markets – such as the TFDPA and the MSCA – has recently been enacted. However, these laws primarily impose obligations on specific businesses operating within narrowly defined sectors, and the scope of regulatory measures available under them is limited. Accordingly, the AMA is still expected to serve as the main instrument for addressing many anticompetitive practices in digital markets.
The JFTC, which is the administrative body responsible for enforcing the AMA, has established the position of Senior Investigator for Digital Platform Operators to handle suspected violations. In addition, it has created the Office of Policy Planning and Research for Digital Markets, which is tasked with supporting activities, including gathering information on actual business practices, considering potential legislative measures and promoting awareness of relevant policies. In recent years, the JFTC has strengthened its institutional capacity by creating new specialist roles in digital areas such as 5G communications, AI, digital advertising and privacy.[3]
Act on Improving Transparency and Fairness of Specified Digital Platforms
The TFDPA[4] came into force on 1 February 2021. The purpose of the Act is to enhance the transparency and fairness of digital platform operations – while respecting the autonomy and self-regulation of platform providers – in order to promote fair and free competition. Like the AMA, the TFDPA functions as part of Japan’s broader competition policy framework, although it falls under the jurisdiction of METI, not the JFTC.
Under the TFDPA, businesses operating online marketplaces or specific types of digital advertising platforms that meet certain thresholds set under the applicable Cabinet Order[5] are designated as Specified Digital Platform Providers.
As of 20 July 2026, the following businesses have been designated as specified digital platform providers:
Table 1: Categories for specified digital platform providers
| Category | Threshold (domestic revenue) | Designated providers | 
|---|---|---|
| General online shopping malls selling goods | ¥300 billion or more | Amazon Japan GK; Rakuten Group, Inc; LY Corporation; eBay Japan GK | 
| Media-integrated digital advertising platform | ¥100 billion or more | Google LLC; Meta Platforms, Inc; LY Corporation; TikTok Pte Ltd | 
| Advertising intermediary digital platform | ¥50 billion or more | Google LLC | 
These specified digital platform providers are required to take measures to ensure transparency and fairness in market conditions vis-à-vis other businesses that sell or operate on their platforms. These obligations include:
- the duty to disclose terms and conditions of transactions;[6]
- the duty to take necessary measures to promote mutual understanding;[7] and
- the duty to submit regular reports to METI.[8]
The TFDPA adopts a “co-regulation” approach, under which the government sets out only the overall regulatory framework while leaving the specifics of compliance to the voluntary efforts of businesses, thereby minimising government intervention and regulatory burden. At the same time, unlike the MSCA, the Act does not contain concrete prohibitions on specific types of conduct, such as self-preferencing.
The Minister of METI, who is responsible for administering the TFDPA, is empowered not only to issue recommendations for improvement in response to violations, but also to issue binding orders in certain cases of non-compliance – failure to comply with which may result in criminal penalties.
Furthermore, if METI identifies conduct that may potentially constitute a violation of the AMA, it may request the JFTC to take appropriate action under the AMA.
Since mid-2024, two formal recommendation cases and one case involving a request to the JFTC for enforcement action have been publicly announced in quick succession.[9]
With respect to app stores – one of the business sectors previously covered by the TFDPA – regulatory authority was shifted towards enforcement by the JFTC under the MSCA since 18 December 2025.
Act on Promotion of Competition for Specified Smartphone Software[10]
The Act on Promotion of Competition for Specified Smartphone Software (MSCA) was enacted on 12 June 2024 and is scheduled to come into full effect on 18 December 2025. (Provisions concerning the designation of regulated businesses, however, came into force earlier on 19 December 2024.)
Often referred to as Japan’s equivalent of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, the MSCA applies to a narrowly defined set of business sectors and operators. Nevertheless, it establishes some specific prohibitions and imposes significantly heavier economic penalties on violators than those under the AMA.
Act against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations (UPMRA)
Advertising regulation in digital markets is dealt with in the AMA and the Act against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations (UPMRA). Following the establishment of the Consumer Affairs Agency (CAA) in 2009, administrative responsibility for the UPMRA was transferred from the JFTC to the CAA.
The UPMRA regulates the offering of excessive prizes and misleading advertisements, where such conduct may interfere with consumers’ ability to make independent and rational purchasing decisions.
Recently, advertising practices in digital markets – particularly “stealth marketing” – have drawn considerable attention. As businesses have become more active in their online advertising efforts, problems have emerged in that advertisements are disguised and not clearly labelled as such, making it difficult for consumers to recognise them as business-originated content.
In response to this situation, the CAA published a report from its Study Group on Stealth Marketing.[11] Based on this report, on 28 March 2023, the Prime Minister issued a public notice designating certain representations as those that “make it difficult for a general consumer to distinguish that the content originates from a business”.[12] At the same time, the CAA released the Operational Guidelines on “Representations That Make It Difficult for Consumers to Identify the Advertiser”.[13]
Enforcement actions relating to violations of the UPMRA in connection with stealth marketing have been actively pursued. Notably, there have also been formal findings of violations based on stealth marketing with respect to advertisements published on businesses’ own websites.
Act on the Protection of Consumers Who Use Digital Platforms for Shopping
Last, although this article does not examine it in detail, the Act on the Protection of Consumers Who Use Digital Platforms for Shopping (PCDPA) came into force on 1 May 2022. The Act is administered by the CAA.
Digital platform providers falling within the definition set out in the Act are subject to certain obligations with respect to the following matters; however, these are limited to best-efforts duties (article 3):[14]
- facilitating smooth communication between consumers and providers offering goods or services via the digital platform;
- investigating and responding to consumer complaints regarding the display of sales terms set by providers; and
- verifying the identity of providers.
Enactment of the MSCA
Purpose of the MSCA
The MSCA was enacted in response to the recommendations made in the Final Report on Competition Assessment of the Mobile Ecosystem, published by the Digital Market Competition Council in June 2023.[15]

articles.title: What is an EU 'associate member'? Why is Canada the first? - AOL.com
articles.summary: What is an EU 'associate member'? Why is Canada the first?  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
Addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said she wanted to bring the relationship “to the highest level possible” in this “openly hostile world”.
Canada has been getting closer to the EU as relations with Washington cooled under Trump. Trade talks collapsed in August 2026, and Trump responded with aggressive 25% to 50% tariffs on Canadian goods. He also threatened their sovereignty, with comments about absorbing Canada and making it “the 51st US state”.
For geographical reasons, Canada cannot turn to full EU membership, so the European Commission is proposing a new “associate member” status. Since it doesn’t exist in the EU treaties, its legal and institutional shape remains unclear.
“What exactly will it be? That will gradually be defined from a legal point of view,” MEP Javier Moreno Sánchez, chair of the Parliament’s Delegation for relations with Canada, told Euronews.
Unlike a simple free-trade partner, Canada would integrate directly into Europe's defence industrial base, participate in joint Arctic projects, cooperate on AI, cyber resilience, and quantum computing, and potentially align on financial services.
It wouldn’t acquire voting rights in the European Parliament or have a say in core EU laws.
A pre-existing partnership
Relations between Canada and the EU were already friendly, stable, and transactional.
In 2016, they signed two key treaties: the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and the Strategic Partnership Agreement (SPA). The first removed 98% of tariffs, boosting bilateral goods and services trade by over 80% to €130 billion. The second focused on foreign policy dialogue and allowed the EU and Canada to hold routine talks on climate change, research, and human rights.
Carney’s victory in 2025 upgraded the relationship with the launch of the “New EU-Canada Strategic Partnership of the Future”. The EU began treating Canada less like a distant trading partner, with both sides aligning on critical mineral supply chains, electric vehicle batteries, clean energy, and Arctic projects. Canada is also an active participant in Horizon Europe, the EU's flagship scientific research program.
In February 2026, Canada became the first non-European country to join the €150 billion SAFE Instrument, allowing Canadian defence firms to bid on joint European military procurement contracts. Canada also became a third-party contributor to PESCO (Permanent Structured Cooperation) military mobility and logistics projects.
Canada’s number one exporter remains the US, which accounted for 72.5% of its merchandise exports in 2025, compared with 12.4% for Europe and Central Asia.
CETA remains stalled, as 10 of 27 EU member states still refuse to fully ratify it. Countries including Italy, France, and Poland argue that Canada has lower environmental and production standards in areas like farming (or like using chemical pesticides and GMOs that are restricted or banned in the EU.)
The proposal
None of the parties is considering Canada joining the EU. The aim is to deepen the economic and strategic partnership beyond the current level of cooperation.
“We know it's a deeper partnership, but less than full membership. Where exactly it's going to be on that spectrum will have to be negotiated. The expectation is that it’s more than a free trade agreement”, said Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre.
The idea is to build on CETA and develop it into an “Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space”, as President von der Leyen said. While the details remain unknown, the partnership is expected to cover policies spanning manufacturing, energy, minerals, AI, quantum computing, and cybersecurity. An Arctic “joint flagship project”, a tech alliance and an integrated defence industrial base are included too.
PM Mark Carney suggested moving “toward seamless, digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”, while also considering a more integrated financial services market.
For Zuleeg, the partnership will primarily focus on geopolitical cohesion and is therefore a “win-win situation”. “It's about like-minded countries coming together, finding common solutions to the big challenges which we are all collectively facing, including a rather difficult situation with the US”, he told Euronews.
Trading resources
This alliance is partly a survival mechanism for Canada. The triggers were the collapse of bilateral trade negotiations with the US, on which roughly 70% of Canada’s export economy relies, and Trump’s threats of absorption.
Moreno Sánchez said Canadian officials had described the breakdown in unusually personal terms. “They explained that geography cannot be changed. They felt betrayed because it was their neighbour, the brother at their doorstep, and then one day it says to them: ‘I don’t want you anymore.’ It affected them very badly.”
The bloc lost access to cheap Russian energy and faces rising tensions with China, so it needs a stable source of critical materials.
“Canada has everything,” Moreno Sánchez said. “It is the second-largest country in the world. Energy, gas, critical raw materials. Obviously, it is in our interest to trade with them.”
Canada holds major reserves of lithium, nickel, cobalt and rare earths, all central to the EU’s energy transition and battery supply chains.
“Until now, with Russian gas and with China, things worked differently,” Moreno Sánchez said. “But now that international relations have become tenser, and we don’t know how this world order will result. It seems like it could become the law of the strongest, that makes you wake up and say: ‘We need to look at this differently.’”
He pointed to Germany as a warning. “Look at what happened in Germany. They relied on Russian gas. When it was cut off, they shut down their nuclear power plants and had no alternative. Now they are burning coal to generate electricity, which is exactly what we should not be doing.”
How it could benefit Europeans
Depending on how partners define “associate membership”, it will have concrete effects on Europeans. The most significant impact would be in the energy sector, according to Dr Giuseppe Spatafora, policy analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies.
“I assume that Canadian energy exports to the EU would alleviate the pressure on the EU’s energy market, increasing supply and reducing dependency on other suppliers”. However, this will take time, as Canada lacks the infrastructure to export large quantities of its energy outside of North America and the appetite to build new pipelines or export terminals, he added.
Removing investment barriers would open the door to new companies, Spatafora explained, while stronger defence cooperation could create new jobs and help protect both European and Canadian societies.
Canada is rich in lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, and copper, key components for many sectors, from batteries and electric vehicles to electronics and medicine. Having Canada as a “safe supplier” would help EU companies keep operating while reducing the leverage of countries like the US and China.
“Canada would certainly be a much safer supplier than China. Whether this translates into a revival of the car industry, I’m not sure, given China’s control of the entire supply chain. But it can certainly help the EU’s efforts to develop strategic industries such as defence and advanced manufacturing”, Spatafora said.
PM Mark Carney proposed strengthening “people-to-people ties” by having Canada participate in the EU’s Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe. This could mean simpler visa rules for European students to study across the Atlantic, as well as joint research and innovation projects.
What’s next?
The EU would need to establish the legal framework for “associate membership” from scratch, defining both parties’ rights and obligations. Major challenges could include aligning partners' regulations and securing unanimous approval from all 27 member states.
Zuleeg hopes the upcoming EU-Canada summit in Montreal on 29-30 October will clarify the term and turn the EU's offer into a concrete proposal. “Negotiations are ongoing. From my perspective, it would be a missed opportunity if, by the October meeting, we don't have concrete progress on the table”, he told Euronews.
Successful headway could raise the question of whether Canada is a one-off case or whether the EU could establish this as a new type of partnership for other countries.
The partnership with Canada could be the “seed” of a “much broader alliance between like-minded countries working together” that can have a multiplying effect, Zuleeg explained. “If we show a united front between the EU, Canada, the UK, Norway, Iceland, but also countries like Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and South Korea, then we really have a critical mass, which will be difficult to ignore even for the US and China”, he added.
Stronger cooperation with close non-European partners would not harm candidate countries’ path to full membership or replace it with associate status. Moreno Sánchez explained that “enlargement has its own path, and relations with reliable partners have their own path” and that these are “happening in parallel”.

articles.full_text:
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.
Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.
Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".
Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.
Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.
Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.
So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?
Spain accused of self-interest
Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.
Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.
"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.
"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."
Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."
Rising Chinese investment
According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.
Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.
China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.
And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.
There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.
"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.
But there's also the question of security.
On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.
"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.
Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".
Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.
"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.
"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."
More emerging alliances
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.
No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.
