articles.title: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets? - BBC
articles.summary: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets?  BBCNew restrictions on food retailers ‘important step’ to better choices – minister  STV NewsFood restrictions to come into force across Glasgow supermarkets today  Glasgow TimesScots face higher shopping bills within days thanks to SNP ban on BOGOF offers  Scottish Daily ExpressHFSS regulations riddle for retailers  Scottish Grocer & Convenience Retailer
articles.full_text:
Sugary soft drinks, biscuits and some breakfast cereals have disappeared from prominent positions in Scotland's supermarkets.
The Scottish government has introduced rules meaning some products that are high in fat, sugar and salt can no longer be put in prime end-of-aisle slots, or feature as part of multi-buy offers in store or online.
The regulations will apply to the usual suspects - chocolate, crisps, biscuits and ice cream.
But it could also include kombucha, seaweed snacks, muesli and chewing gum, depending on their sugar content.
What are the new rules?
The Scottish government regulations apply to businesses with more than 50 employees. This could include supermarkets, high street shops, restaurants, pharmacies, petrol stations and garden centres.
They are are no longer allowed to display pre-packaged foods including sugary soft drinks, confectionery, biscuits and breakfast cereals in prominent locations such as entrances, checkouts, aisle ends and designated queueing areas.
Price promotions on those items - such as "three for the price of two", "three for £10" or "buy five and save 20%" - are no longer allowed.
Multi-buy offers, including extra loyalty points, are also banned.
Another type of deal that falls foul of the rules is those offering a free high-sugar, fat or salt product alongside another purchase - for example, a free chocolate bar with a newspaper.
There are no restrictions on discounts such as half-price or "save £1".
Online retailers also face restrictions - including a ban on advertising some foods on their homepage.
Similar restrictions are already in place in England and Wales.
Chocolate, ice cream... what else?
The short answer is: a lot, if there’s enough sugar, salt or fat packed into it.
The restrictions could apply to:
- Drinks with added sugar - such as lemonade, soda, squash, chocolate milk, almond milk, ready-made coffee, kombucha, energy drinks, and hot chocolate
- Savoury snacks such as crisps and tortilla chips, and even lentil-based crisps and seaweed snacks, depending on their content
- Breakfast cereals, granola, muesli and oat-based cereals
- Pre-made pizzas, roast potatoes, chips, fish fingers and chicken nuggets
- Ready meals, as well as pasta, rice or noodles with added ingredients or fillings, such as ravioli and tortellini
- Confectionary, such as popcorn, chocolate, chewing gum and sweets
- Ice cream, sorbets, ice lollies, sponge cakes, custard, jelly, crumbles
- Cereal bars, biscuits, scones, flapjacks, doughnuts and Danish pastries
- Sweetened Greek-style, probiotic, kids' and drinking yoghurts
Is this the end of the meal deal?
Meal deals are exempt from the regulations, as are "dine for two" offers.
However, any foods identified in the rules, whether part of a meal deal or not, cannot be placed in the restricted locations, such as supermarket entrances.
The fight against obesity
The Scottish government regulations are being introduced to encourage healthier eating choices.
Public Health Minister Maree Todd noted that two out of three Scottish adults are overweight or obese, with those living in the poorest areas worst affected.
She said: "We know that promotions and prominent product placement can encourage over-consumption and impulse buying of foods with high levels of calories, fat, sugar and salt.
"By restricting the promotion of less healthy food and drink we can make it easier for people to make healthier choices, improving health and wellbeing, and create a Scotland where everyone eats well and has a healthy weight."

articles.title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children  The GuardianMove to end charges for parents to sit by children on flights  BBCTake off for passengers as government scraps extra charges when flying  GOV.UKAirlines face crackdown on charging parents to sit with their children  The TimesUK airlines set for major change in policy under new plans  Oxford Mail
articles.full_text:
Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.
The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.
It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.
MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.
Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.
“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”
An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department for Transport.
Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”
Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.
Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found.
Under the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing and have their children alongside them free of charge.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers.
Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.
Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

articles.title: Humilation for Labour as over half of Brits think UK can't defend Putin attack - Daily Express
articles.summary: Humilation for Labour as over half of Brits think UK can't defend Putin attack  Daily Express
articles.full_text:
A bombshell new poll shows the majority of Britons fear the country cannot defend itself from an attack by Russia. In a blow to Labour, more than half (54%) of people who took part in the shocking survey said they are not confident Britain would be able to repel an attack from Vladimir Putin's forces.
It comes as Andy Burnham comes under growing pressure to hike defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. In the survey, 24% of respondents said they were “not at all confident” of Britain’s defences against a Russian military attack, while 30% said they were “not very confident”.
Just over one in three (34%) said they were confident, according to a survey for The i Paper by BMG Research. When broken down, 24% answered they were “fairly confident” and only 10% said “very confident”. Some 13% answered, “don’t know”.
The number of people who took part in the survey was not reported. Experts have long raised concerns over Britain’s ability to defend itself. The country is particularly vulnerable to ballistic missiles, with the Royal Navy’s Sea Viper missile-armed Type 45 destroyers the only layer of defence against the weapons. However, the Navy only has six of the £1 billion warships which have suffered availability issues and are often not deployed.
It is thought Britain would also struggle to fend off waves off Russian drones, as seen regularly in Ukraine. Responding to the survey, retired General Sir Richard Barrons, co-author of last year’s Strategic Defence Review, told The i he “admired the 34 per cent” who were confident in Britain’s ability to stop a Russian attack.
He added: “As the SDR made clear last year, the UK has the Armed Forces it ended up with at the end of the post-Cold War era, yet lives now in a new, far more dangerous era of state confrontation and conflict.”
Mr Burnham has committed to the new NATO target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. He was expected to lay out the roadmap to hitting this figure during his Labour Party conference speech on Wednesday.
However, he did not discuss the plan — prompting criticism from the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats. NATO chief Mark Rutte has warned Russia could attack an alliance member within the next five years.
A Government spokesman said: “We’ve delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War – committing nearly £300bn over the next four years. That means more money for the kit and personnel that keep us safe everyday. And we’ve launched the Home Defence Programme, to ensure we’re prepared for potential threats, however likely they may be. Just weeks ago, we announced that we’ll be updating departmental crisis plans, known as The Warbook, and will be holding the largest home defence exercise in recent UK history next year.”

articles.title: Advocacy Group Stop Killing Games Sounds Alarm On EU Kids Act: ‘This Is Such A Horrible Law Proposal’ - kotaku.com
articles.summary: Advocacy Group Stop Killing Games Sounds Alarm On EU Kids Act: ‘This Is Such A Horrible Law Proposal’  kotaku.comExperts: Social networks need to be made safer for children; a ban is not the solution · BNN  Baltic News NetworkRelational AI for Minors: Where the Evidence Supports Regulation – and Where It Does Not Yet  European ScientistAs the EU debates the KIDS Act, Brazil is already enforcing one  IAPPFirms ’should pay price’ for harm to children &n...
articles.full_text:
In a recently released video, the consumer advocacy group Stop Killing Games and its creator, YouTuber Ross Scott, have expressed concern with the European Union’s recently proposed EU Kids Act, which Scott has referred to as a “bomb that could implode the whole video games industry.”
The EU Kids Act was officially proposed on September 17, 2026. According to the outline provided for the EU Kids Act on the official European Commission website, the proposal in question primarily “seeks to protect minors from risky digital services and AI systems, uphold the digital single market and maintain a coherent regulatory framework and enforcement structure for the protection of minors online.”
However, Stop Killing Games’ Ross Scott stated in a new video that the EU Kids Act is using the ever-looming threat of AI and the protection of “minors from risky digital services” as a “cover” for its true aims, referring to these things as a “mask to hide what else is in there.”
“Curbing social media and AI has nothing to do with why this is such a horrible law proposal,” stated Scott. “As it stands, the EU Kids Act is the most draconian proposal I’ve ever seen regarding video games and consumers.” Among Scott’s chief concerns is that the proposal will “require your personal identifying information to play an online video game” and “make all private game servers illegal.”
While Scott’s comments were initially based on a leaked version of the EU Kids Act proposal, the segments from it featured in his video do line up exactly with the official version of the proposal that has since been published on the European Commission website. Said proposal is indeed quite broad in its application, as it states that it “sets out clear safety by design requirements for online social networking services, video-sharing platform services, online games, AI companions and general conversational chatbots, and software application stores.”
It’s important to bear in mind that the proposal is a 99-page document, and there’s a lot of legalese to contend with. That being said, the main section in question where video games are concerned is Chapter III, titled “Safety By Design.” But, as Scott explains, there’s a confusing wrinkle in this proposal that has to be tackled before we even get to that: how does the EU Kids Act define a “video game”?
According to the “definitions” section of the proposal, a “video game” is “an information society service.” The use of the term “information society service” here is quite specific, as the EU GDPR defines it as “any service normally provided for remuneration, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of a recipient of services.” In simpler terms, an “information society service” is something that can be purchased online.
 All hands on deck! This is the biggest threat to Stop Killing Games yet!
The EU #KidsAct could end #StopKillingGames by collapsing the EU gaming market and making private and community servers illegal!:https://t.co/X4vfKUQVBN
"The best thing you can do is spread the word…The…
— Stop Killing Games Official (@StopKilingGames) September 30, 2026
So, does this apply to digitally purchased games that have no online features? Scott argues that said definition “is as clear as mud,” which is why Stop Killing Games is concerned that the EU Kids Act’s age verification requirements can be broadly applied to any game purchased through a digital storefront. Obviously, this is an extremely pertinent concern considering that Steam is a purely digital storefront, and Sony is ending disc production for all new PlayStation games in 2028.
Of course, the EU Kids Act is in no way final. It is, quite literally, a proposal, which means it’s still in the earliest stage of the European Union’s legislative process. Before it even reaches both the European Parliament’s and the EU Council’s voting stages, it will be reviewed and, most likely, amended.
And, as Scott stated in his conclusion, that’s exactly why Stop Killing Games believes that tackling the EU Kids Act now is a priority: “The best thing you can do is spread the word on this. The people who write this crap do not like it when the public at large knows what they’re trying to do to you. If everyone in gaming understood what the EU Kids Act is trying to do, it wouldn’t have a chance of passing. So, let’s let people know!”

articles.title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Iran’s Remaining Industrial Lifelines - EIN News
articles.summary: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Iran’s Remaining Industrial Lifelines  EIN News
articles.full_text:
Actions Target Iran’s Automotive, Rail, Manufacturing, and Steel Networks
WASHINGTON—Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury is targeting some of the last significant elements of Iran’s failing industrial infrastructure, including its rail and automotive conglomerates. Much like the petroleum sector, Iran’s automotive and rail industries have been coopted by the regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), whose corruption and self‑serving interests have pushed Iran’s economy to the brink.
"The Iranian regime's ability to fund its war machine and inflict terror on the world has been severely diminished thanks to Operation Economic Outcast,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Today’s action directly targets Iran’s enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime’s revenue once and for all.”
As the U.S. military’s maritime blockade takes hold and Iran’s oil revenues fall to zero, the regime has grown increasingly dependent on these remaining industries to maintain a veneer of economic solvency. Because the rail and automotive sectors represent some of the regime’s largest remaining sources of revenue and logistical capacity, today’s action strikes directly at the critical arteries Iran relies on to sustain its economy and evade sanctions.
The automotive sector, in particular, is deeply intertwined with IRGC patronage networks, enabling corruption, trade‑based money laundering, and even the exploitation of prison labor, making the dismantling of these channels vital to cutting off IRGC financing. By reaching not only Iranian firms but also the foreign suppliers and facilitators that nourish them, today’s designations sever the international procurement networks the regime depends on to preserve its industrial base and circumvent U.S. pressure.
As part of today’s action, OFAC is issuing two additional sectoral sanctions determinations pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902 targeting Iran’s automotive and rail sectors. These determinations authorize OFAC to sanction any entity or individual operating in the aforementioned sectors. As such, the designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to E.O. 13902 and E.O. 13871, which targets key Iranian industrial sectors, namely its iron, steel, aluminum, or copper sector.
OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME
Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime. Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror. Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. The United States is seeing results as Iranian airlines lose access to airports overseas and as foreign countries work to close off Iran’s financial access.
Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran. Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. It also expanded secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here.
IRANIAN AUTOMOTIVE SECTOR
Iran’s automotive sector, Iran’s largest economic sector outside of oil and gas, remains a core contributor to Iran’s industrial base and is a major revenue generator for the regime. Though riddled with corruption and mismanagement—Iran’s automotive sector loses over $1 billion annually—the sector remains an essential component of Iran’s defense industrial base and a lucrative cash cow for the IRGC to siphon funds from an ostensibly commercial venture. While Iranian automakers claim to have a resilient, homegrown automotive manufacturing base, in reality, low-quality vehicles are often imported from third countries and rebranded under local Iranian brand names.
Two main companies represent over 90 percent of Iran’s domestic auto market: Iran Khodro Company (IKCO), which maintains close ties to the IRGC, and SAIPA Iranian Automobile Manufacturing Company (SAIPA). IKCO is Iran’s largest automaker and one of the largest automobile manufacturers in the Middle East. SAIPA is Iran’s second largest automaker, together with IKCO producing nearly 1,500,000 vehicles annually. Iran Khodro Diesel is an IKCO subsidiary and is Iran’s largest manufacturer of buses, trucks, and diesel engines. Pars Khodro Company and Zamyad Company are SAIPA subsidiaries responsible for manufacturing passenger and commercial cars, respectively.
Niroo Motor Shiraz Industrial and Manufacturing Company (Niroo Motor Shiraz), Iran’s largest motorcycle manufacturer and part of the Niroo Motor Group, uses prison labor for manufacturing and has closely cooperated with the IRGC and Basij, including supplying over 6,000 motorcycles for use by plainclothes intelligence agents on patrol. Niroo Motor Damavand Company is a subsidiary of the Niroo Motor Group.
Iran Khodro Company, SAIPA Iranian Automobile Manufacturing Company, Iran Khodro Diesel Company, Pars Khodro Company, Zamyad Company, Niroo Motor Shiraz Industrial and Manufacturing Company, and Niroo Motor Damavand Company are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the automotive sector of the Iranian economy.
AUTO INDUSTRY FOREIGN SUPPLIERS
Companies in the Middle East and East Asia continue to export key automotive parts to sustain Iran’s auto industry and evade U.S. sanctions. Indonesia-based PT Golden Motorcycle International (PT Golden) has engaged in multiple shipments of auto parts to Niroo Motor Damavand Company.
UAE-based Integrated Auto Parts LLC has facilitated multiple auto parts shipments via UAE to Iran, importing parts transshipped from foreign companies in Turkiye and India.
Turkiye-based Troy Trading Arac Parcalari Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi has sent truck parts to Bahman Diesel Co., a subsidiary of sanctioned Iranian auto manufacturer Bahman Group, who produces heavy trucks and other work vehicles for the Iranian armed forces, including the IRGC and its unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and missile divisions.
Hong Kong-based Hessenberg Co., Limited, also known as Jedburgh Co., Limited, and Tanex Global Trading Hong Kong Limited have supplied Iran’s largest auto manufacturers, including IKCO and SAIPA, with auto parts.
PT Golden Motorcycle International, Integrated Auto Parts LLC, Troy Trading Arac Parcalari Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi, Hessenberg Co., Limited, and Tanex Global Trading Hong Kong Limited are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the automotive sector of the Iranian economy.
IRANIAN RAIL SECTOR
Iran has turned in desperation to its rail sector to help sustain its economy in the face of the U.S. military’s maritime blockade, including to transport oil and sustain regional trade. Key Iranian rail companies include the Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company (RAI), a state-owned railroad company which provides passenger and freight services, and the Raja Passenger Trains Company, which took over certain passenger business from RAI and serves as a primary passenger rail company to domestic and limited overseas destinations. Sherkat-E Rah Ahan-E Khamle-O-Naghle, also known as the Railway Transportation Company, is a key private freight company sustaining some notable railway activities.
Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company, Raja Passenger Trains Company, and Sherkat-E Rah Ahan-E Khamle-O-Naghle are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the rail sector of the Iranian economy.
MANUFACTURING, MINING, AND METALS
The Iranian metals industry is second only to its petroleum industry in terms of the value of exports, making it an important revenue source for the regime. Iran utilizes overseas companies to source materials for its homegrown industrial base, and for the purpose of selling its sanctioned goods to foreign buyers.
Iran-based Heavy Equipment Production Company (HEPCO) is one of the Middle East’s largest manufacturers of mining and road construction machinery, producing thousands of bulldozers, excavators, and other machines annually. HEPCO’s products have been utilized by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF) to build and improve military training sites, and by the IRGC to construct underground facilities.
HEPCO Shanghai Co., Ltd (HEPCO Shanghai) serves as HEPCO’s China-based subsidiary, through which it procures raw materials and other parts for its parent company’s manufacturing hub in Iran.
Heavy Equipment Production Company is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the manufacturing sector of the Iranian economy, while HEPCO Shanghai Co., Ltd is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, HEPCO.
UAE-based Silver Line Metal Trading LLC sells stainless steel products to Iranian steel producers. French students have set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.
Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.

Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.
At Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school, the teachers were inadvertently splashed as a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. Earlier, the prosecutor’s office had said the teachers had been assaulted and “doused in petrol”.
At another school in the city, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a firetruck that had arrived to put out a blaze in the morning, police said. The attackers forced the firefighters to flee the vehicle, then set it alight.
In Nantes, firefighters extinguished a fire at a high school entrance following what regional education officials called a gathering “marked by violence towards staff”. In Strasbourg, trams were halted to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, and students burned barriers on tram tracks, authorities said.
“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius [95 degrees Fahrenheit] in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael, a 17-year-old who withheld his surname for fear of reprisals, told the AFP news agency outside a protest in Strasbourg.
“The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors.”
His frustration echoes a wave of student anger that has spread across France since last week, as high school pupils protest and grievances snowball into nationwide unrest.
Some 340 demonstrations were under way outside high schools by mid-morning on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down as a result, police said.
University students joined in, blocking access to about 30 campuses, including in Paris and Marseille, according to a student union.
Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries – some from thrown objects, others reportedly from police riot-control projectiles.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police have opened internal investigations into brutality allegations involving three students.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting and asked ministers to cancel upcoming official travel so authorities could focus on the demonstrations, his office said.
French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that he would successively meet representative staff unions and parent and student associations on Friday.
The unrest has become entangled in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron next May. The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed party of encouraging the protests. Presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Wednesday that his party “called for nonviolent methods of struggle” and criticised the government’s response as repressive.

articles.title: Europe went all in on soft power for too long, Belgian defence minister says - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Europe went all in on soft power for too long, Belgian defence minister says  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
In an interview with Euronews, the Belgian defence minister argued that Europe spent too long focusing on soft power instead of defence.
Both when it comes to defence capabilities and industry capacities, Europe is in a very difficult position, Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken told Euronews. He pointed to the bloc's decades-long prioritising of soft power as one reason for this.
His comments come as the European NATO members are ramping up defence spending and Brussels is rolling out policies to bolster the defence industry. While Francken sees progress being made, he warned Europe does not have all the capabilities it needs.
"Europe has been very good at investing in soft power, in social security, and it's beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems," Francken said in an interview at Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.
"When somebody gets sick, when somebody has lost his job, we have everything. But when there's war or when there is a hybrid threat, we don't have anything."
He noted that when it comes specifically to defence spending, Belgium has long been the bad apple.
"We neglected this for so long, we were like the worst pupil in NATO class," Francken said, again, referring to the emphasis put on soft power.
"We are the founding father of NATO; we're the founding father of the EU. I think that we always were there for diplomacy, for soft power, but when we talked hard power in Belgium, everybody was looking in the other direction."
Belgium reached NATO's 2% GDP defence spending threshold for the first time in 2025, rising from a low of 0.97% in 2014.
NATO wants that percentage to reach 3.5% by 2035; however, the country will remain at 2% until 2029 due to its challenging budgetary climate. Belgium currently has one of the worst budget deficits in the eurozone.
"Now we doubled the budget; we reached 2%. I know that we add two more, but it's quite a process. We're doing so much, but I cannot undo in 18 months of being a minister what has been neglected for 40 years."

articles.title: Digital Assets + Blockchain Newsletter – October 1, 2026 - Consumer Financial Services Law Monitor
articles.summary: Digital Assets + Blockchain Newsletter – October 1, 2026  Consumer Financial Services Law Monitor
articles.full_text:
Welcome to the first issue of the Digital Assets + Blockchain Newsletter. In this newsletter, we’ll track the regulatory, legislative, and enforcement developments reshaping the crypto and digital assets landscape — from the GENIUS Act’s stablecoin framework to the SEC’s and CFTC’s evolving posture on digital commodities to custody rules, licensing regimes, and beyond.
In This Issue:
In the Spotlight
In the Wake of CLARITY Act’s Failure, Agencies Move Forward Without Congressional Action or Certainty
After the Senate blocked the CLARITY Act, Troutman Pepper Locke’s Genna Garver and David Madrazo examine how the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) are moving to fill the regulatory gap on their own, from the SEC’s proposed Regulation Crypto Assets to updated CFTC guidance on tokenized investments, and where agency action reaches its limits, particularly on bankruptcy protections for digital asset customers. Click here to read the full article.
Troutman Pepper Locke to Attend The Bridge Conference in New York
Members of Troutman Pepper Locke’s Digital Assets and Blockchain team, Akshay Belani, Genna Garver, Deb Kovosky, and Ethan Ostroff, will attend The Bridge, an invitation-only institutional crypto conference in New York on October 27. Organized by The Tie, the event gathers 600+ institutions and 1,100+ attendees for high-level panels and private meetings on tokenization, DeFi, and digital asset markets.
Federal Developments
September 25, SEC Corp Fin Staff Issues FAQs on Crypto Asset Classification and Investment Contract Analysis Under March 2026 Interpretive Release
The SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance issued staff-level FAQs interpreting the Commission’s March 17, 2026 Interpretive Release on the application of federal securities laws to crypto assets, expressly noting the FAQs are staff views only, carry no legal force, and do not bind the Commission.
The guidance addresses two groups of questions: classification issues under Section III of the Interpretive Release, including that an issuer’s own stated definitions of “functionality” and “decentralization” (not the Release’s general definitions) govern whether the issuer has fulfilled its representations, that Staking Receipt Tokens may be classified as either a “digital tool” or a “digital commodity” depending on whether they are issued by a protocol-based Liquid Staking Provider, and that a “receipt” is distinguished from other instruments by the issuer’s inability to transfer, lend, pledge, rehypothecate, or otherwise use the deposited asset; and investment-contract issues under Section IV, including when marketing communications constitute representations of “essential managerial efforts,” confirmation that a non-security crypto asset does not separate from its associated investment contract merely because a third party assumes the issuer’s promised efforts, that services to secure, maintain, or improve an already-functional crypto system do not constitute essential managerial efforts, that statements by an issuer of a functional, centerless crypto system generally cannot create a new investment contract, and that buyback program announcements are not representations of managerial efforts where the system is functional and has no central party but may be where the system is not yet functional and the buyback is framed as generating yield.
For more information, click here.

September 24, FRB Proposes Two Rules Implementing GENIUS Act Stablecoin Framework for State Member Banks
The Federal Reserve Board (FRB) requested public comment on two proposed rules governing payment stablecoin issuance under the GENIUS Act. The first sets the ongoing substantive framework for FRB-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) and related custodians, covering permissible activities, one-to-one reserve backing in cash, short-term Treasuries, and other permissible assets, two-business-day redemption and fee disclosure requirements, monthly audited reserve reporting with CEO/CFO certifications, standardized capital requirements, and a cross-cutting anti-tying prohibition that reaches all PPSIs regardless of regulator. The second establishes a tailored application process for insured state member banks seeking to issue stablecoins through a subsidiary, including a 30-day completeness review, a 120-day decision deadline (with deemed approval if missed), safety-and-soundness-based denial standards, and an appeals process. The proposals are closely coordinated with parallel Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) rulemakings, and comments on both are due 60 days after Federal Register publication. For more information, click here.
September 24, CFTC Staff Updates FAQs on Registrant Use of Tokenized Collateral and Blockchain Recordkeeping
The CFTC’s Market Participants Division, Division of Market Oversight, and Division of Clearing and Risk (Release Number 9303-26) released updates to their FAQs Concerning Registrant and Registered Entity Activities Relating to Crypto Assets and Blockchain Technologies, addressing two new topics: investment of customer funds in tokenized forms of permitted investments, and the use of blockchain technology to satisfy registrants’ recordkeeping requirements. Chairman Michael S. Selig said the update reflects the agency’s “ongoing efforts to provide regulatory clarity for the crypto industry.” The FAQs, first issued March 20, 2026, build on and provide further clarity regarding CFTC Staff Letter 25-39 (Tokenized Collateral Guidance) and CFTC Staff Letter 26-05 (the staff no-action position on digital assets accepted as margin collateral). For more information, click here.
September 21, SEC Grants ARK Venture Fund Relief for a Tokenized Share Class
In Investment Company Act Release No. 36333 (File No. 812-16031), the Commission granted ARK Venture Fund and ARK Investment Management exemptions from §§ 18(a)(2), 18(c), and 18(i), Rule 23c-3, and Section 17(d) and Rule 17d-1 so the closed-end interval fund can offer two new classes alongside its existing shares: an Exchange Class listed on a national securities exchange and a Tokenized Class traded on alternative trading systems or other quotation mediums. The relief is subject to the conditions in the application. ARK has not announced a launch. It is the first 1940 Act exemptive order built around a tokenized class, and it lands three weeks after the SEC’s transfer-agent proposal and four days after the Innovation Exemption. For more information, click here.
September 18, OCC Grants Conditional Trust Charters to Bastion, Catena, and Agora
The OCC granted conditional national trust charters to fintechs Bastion Platforms, Catena Trust Bank, and Agora National Trust Bank, each seeking to expand stablecoin and crypto offerings.
Bastion converts its existing New York trust company into a national trust company and will pursue white-label stablecoin issuance, fiduciary wallet services, and issuer services; Catena, a new entity and subsidiary of AI-agent banking platform Catena Labs, will offer custody, investment management, conversion, and clearing/execution across fiat, securities, stablecoins and crypto; and Agora, issuer of the AUSD token, will focus on stablecoin issuance, reserve maintenance, and institutional custody services.
All three must limit activities to trust-company business and secure Federal Reserve bank stock before full approval.
The Bank Policy Institute and Independent Community Bankers of America objected to Catena’s and Agora’s applications as insufficiently detailed and potentially exceeding trust-company activities (including possible unregistered brokerage for Catena), but the OCC found both firms followed established procedures and that commenters had adequate opportunity to respond.
The approvals continue the OCC’s expansive posture toward crypto trust charters (following Fidelity Digital Assets, Coinbase, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial) even as it has denied others (Bunq, Wise US) and reflect the charter’s growing appeal under the GENIUS Act, which named the OCC as primary regulator of stablecoin issuers.
For more information, click here, here, and here.

September 17, SEC Issues Five-Year “Innovation Exemption” for Onchain Trading of Tokenized NMS Stocks
The Commission granted temporary conditional relief under Exchange Act § 36(a)(1) that lets “tokenized securities venues” trade tokenized National Market System (NMS) stocks through permissioned automated market makers and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges. Liquidity providers that fund those pools with their own capital are exempt from the “dealer” definition. Conditions include limits on the number of symbols and on volume, tokens that carry the same rights as the underlying stock, notice to the issuer before a venue lists a third-party tokenized version of its shares, auditable smart contracts on a public permissionless ledger, halts that track the primary listing exchange, and public disclosure of operations and trading activity. The relief runs five years from publication, and the order asks for public comment. The issuer-notice condition follows AMC’s September 3 objection to tokens referencing its shares without consent. September 17, CFTC Sends Crypto Market Rulemaking to White House Review Two Days After the CLARITY Vote
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) received a CFTC rulemaking titled “Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets” (RIN 3038-AF80) on Sept 17. articles.title: US sanctions Iran’s major automakers, rail and metals firms - Aaj English TV
articles.summary: US sanctions Iran’s major automakers, rail and metals firms  Aaj English TV
articles.full_text:
The United States on Thursday announced fresh sanctions targeting Iran’s largest automakers, as well as major rail, manufacturing and metals companies, as Washington seeks to exert maximum pressure in its war against the country.
The US Treasury said the measures target sectors that represent some of Iran’s largest remaining sources of revenue and logistical capacity.
“Because the rail and automotive sectors represent some of the regime’s largest remaining sources of revenue and logistical capacity, today’s action strikes directly at the critical arteries Iran relies on to sustain its economy and evade sanctions,” the US Treasury said in a statement.
The new sanctions target Iran’s two largest automakers, Iran Khodro (IKCO) and SAIPA, which serve the domestic market and export to regional trading partners.
In total, seven automakers were sanctioned under Washington’s so-called “Operation Economic Outcast”, launched as part of its drive to cut off the Iranian government’s sources of revenue.
Niroo Motor, Iran’s largest motorcycle manufacturer, was also sanctioned.
The measures also targeted international partners of Iran’s auto sector, including Indonesia’s Golden Motorcycle Company and auto parts companies in the United Arab Emirates, Turkiye and Hong Kong.
Key Iranian rail companies sanctioned include state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company (RAI), Raja Passenger Trains Company and private freight carrier Sherkat-E Rah Ahan-E Khamle-O-Naghle.
The sanctions also targeted major steel and manufacturing companies in Iran, including Heavy Equipment Production Company (HEPCO), described by the US Treasury as one of the Middle East’s largest manufacturers of mining and road construction machinery.
Washington also sanctioned HEPCO’s Shanghai-based subsidiary, as well as companies in the United Arab Emirates and Germany accused of aiding Iranian steel companies.
The new measures also targeted a steel and oil export network run by two Hong Kong-based Iranian-Dominican nationals.

articles.summary: Elon Musk returns to Trump administration to co-lead Pentagon war study  Euronews.comHegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors  The GuardianPentagon creates 'Autowarcom' to expand AI and drone capabilities  ReutersElon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to help Pentagon with warfare initiative, Hegseth says  CNBCElon Musk to return his attention to government, advise Pentagon on future of war  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
Musk, who in 2024 threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he spearheaded sweeping job cuts across the US federal government.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump's government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war.
Musk served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he oversaw sweeping job cuts across the US federal government, before departing in May 2025.
In a speech Wednesday at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said "Project Meridian" will be "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare." "We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists", he added.
Musk will be a co-leader of Project Meridian alongside Palmer Luckey, the 34-year-old co founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries, and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year old Republican former House speaker.
No stranger to the Pentagon
Musk's companies are already major Pentagon contractors, including SpaceX building satellite networks for Trump's planned "Golden Dome" missile defence shield. His artificial intelligence firm xAI this year signed a deal allowing the military to use its Grok chatbot on classified systems.
In 2024, Musk threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, but the men later had a high-profile blow-up over the president's spending legislation.
The two have since reconciled, and Musk has again become a frequent presence at the White House, though less visibly than during his previous stint, when he often visited the Oval Office, most memorably with his young son on his shoulders.
On Tuesday he was seated next to Trump at a lunch with artificial intelligence executives, where he joined other tech leaders in signing a voluntary AI safety accord that the president described as "morally binding."
Last week, Musk attended the state dinner Trump hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in May he flew to Beijing on Air Force One as part of the business delegation accompanying Trump on his state visit to China.
Back among the big donors
He also resumed giving to Republican causes, including multimillion-dollar donations to individual candidates and conservative political groups. Musk, who spent more than $250 million backing Trump and other Republicans in the 2024 election, has given at least $90 million toward November's midterm elections, according to tallies of Federal Election Commission filings.
Hegseth said the project's purpose is to "creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master." Project members will include hand-picked private sector leaders and subject matter experts from across the innovation, academic and policy ecosystems. Hegseth said he has directed Project Meridian's findings to be completed and submitted within 120 days.

EUR/USD extends its decline on Thursday, falling to its lowest level since May 2025 and setting a fresh year-to-date low as the US Dollar remains firmly supported by elevated US Treasury yields and resilient US economic data. At the time of writing, the pair trades around 1.1253, down 0.67% on the day.
The US Dollar Index, which measures the Greenback against a basket of six major currencies, holds near 101.80 after reaching a fresh yearly high of 101.99. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield trades around 5.30%, close to the 5.34% peak reached earlier in the day, its highest level since 2002.
The US ISM Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) edged down to 54.5 in September from 54.6, missing the 55.0 forecast but staying comfortably above the 50.0 mark that separates expansion from contraction. The Prices Paid Index, however, jumped to 77.9 from 71.1, well above expectations of 72.3.
The US labour market also remains firm. Initial Jobless Claims fell to 197K in the week ending September 26, below the 200K forecast and the previous reading of 198K. The four-week moving average declined to 200K from 202.5K. The data follows Wednesday’s ADP report, which showed that private-sector employment increased by 90K in September, beating expectations of 70K and rising sharply from 36K in August.
The latest figures suggest that the US economy remains strong enough for the Fed to maintain a tight monetary policy stance. However, the CME FedWatch Tool shows that traders see only about a 36% chance that the central bank will raise interest rates at its October meeting after the Fed’s preferred inflation measure showed some moderation.
Core Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation rose 0.2% MoM in August, below the 0.3% forecast, while the annual rate remained unchanged at 3.0%, undershooting expectations of 3.3%. Even so, inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, while elevated energy prices keep the risks tilted to the upside as US-Iran negotiations remain deadlocked.
Fed policymakers continue to signal concern about inflation. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid said on Thursday, “Officials have work to do on inflation,” adding that “energy prices are one of the biggest challenges for monetary policy today.” Boston Fed President Susan Collins said, “Economic growth is near trend, if not more than that; labor market near full employment, but inflation is too high.”
On the European side, stronger Eurozone manufacturing activity offers limited support to the Euro (EUR). The final HCOB Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.9 in September from 52.7, reaching its highest level since May 2022.
On the monetary policy front, the European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice this year, while markets are pricing in additional tightening as inflation remains elevated. Preliminary data released on Wednesday showed that inflation in several major Eurozone economies accelerated more than expected in September. However, policymakers have also acknowledged downside risks to growth, which could keep the ECB cautious about raising rates aggressively. Traders now turn their attention to Friday’s preliminary Eurozone inflation report and US Nonfarm Payrolls data.

UK and Jersey police assisting murder inquiry
Police investigating the suspected murder of a woman in Alderney are receiving assistance from officers in Jersey and the UK.
Hannah Benfield, 34, was found in the sea at the base of cliffs in the west of the island on Monday and a 44-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of her murder.
States of Jersey Police said it had deployed five specialist search officers to Alderney following a "standard mutual aid" request, while other officers are assisting from the south-west of the UK and Guernsey Customs and Immigration, said Guernsey Police.
Chief officer Damian Kitchen said the investigation had been a "complex" process requiring "meticulous work".
Kitchen said the inquiry was placing pressure on the force and he asked islanders to be patient as officers managed competing demands.
"Our officers and staff are committed to being there when needed and will always respond immediately where there is a threat to life, a risk of harm, or a crime in progress," he said.
Kitchen said assistance from other forces would continue "into the weekend and beyond".
He thanked the Alderney community for its "help, welcome and support" during what he described as an "incredibly unsettling time".

articles.title: Q&A: AWS’ Sasha Rubel on AI Regulation & European Healthcare - Healthcare Digital
articles.summary: Q&A: AWS’ Sasha Rubel on AI Regulation & European Healthcare  Healthcare Digital
articles.full_text:
Sasha Rubel leads AI Policy across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Amazon Web Services (AWS).
Working with governments to support their understanding of what AI means in practice and helping technology leaders navigate the rules shaping how AI is built and deployed, Sasha is on the frontline of AI policy across the EMEA region.
Before joining AWS, Sasha gained deep experience in international affairs, spending over a decade at UNESCO, including positions in Ethiopia and Senegal.
Following her time on the African continent, Sasha returned to France with UNESCO to lead the organisation’s global work across AI, innovation, data governance, digital inclusion and digital transformation.
Today, a significant portion of her work involves advising governments and technology leaders about AI regulation and deployment in the healthcare sector, where “the consequences of getting AI right – or wrong – can be profound,” says Sasha.
Sasha shared her insights with Healthcare Digital on the state of play across the European regulatory landscape and where the opportunities and barriers for widespread AI adoption in healthcare lie.
What is Europe getting right on AI adoption in healthcare policy - and is the balance wrong anywhere?
SR: Our new data from an AWS-commissioned report, ‘Unlocking Europe’s AI Potential’, based on a survey of more than 34,000 European organisations, businesses, and citizens, shows incredible momentum and opportunity for AI adoption in the healthcare space.
AI adoption in healthcare is still below the European business average - 41% compared with 54%. But among healthcare organisations that are adopting AI, use is more sophisticated than in any other sector: 55% are consistently using multiple AI tools. Healthcare is also leading on AI governance, with 36% of organisations having a formal AI strategy.
Taken together, this suggests a more deliberate approach to adoption: healthcare organisations may be moving more slowly, but those that do adopt AI are putting the governance and strategy in place alongside deployment, rather than deploying first and addressing the risks later. In a sector where patient safety and clinical trust are at stake, that disciplined approach matters.
“Among healthcare organisations that are adopting AI, use is more sophisticated than in any other sector. ”
Where the balancing act becomes challenging isn’t this caution itself, but the complex regulatory environment innovators have to navigate. For example, a clinical AI tool supporting diagnostic decisions is faced with answering several differing compliance regimes, all at the same time.
It may need to obtain CE marking under the medical device framework, ensure that any processing of patient data complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and meet the requirements that apply to high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act. Each has its own authority, compliance obligations and enforcement path.
Over half of healthcare organisations say that compliance spend has risen significantly – more than any sector – and that spend is going toward reconciling overlapping rules rather than towards life-saving innovation and deployment.
Europe hasn’t matched its adoption rates with an equally coordinated and mainstreamed regulatory pathway, and that gap is absorbing resources and momentum that would otherwise translate directly into patient impact.
- 41% of healthcare organisations are adopting AI, compared with 54% across European businesses overall.
- 55% of healthcare organisations using AI are consistently deploying multiple AI tools – the highest proportion of any sector.
- 36% of healthcare organisations have a formal AI strategy, putting healthcare ahead of other sectors on AI governance.
- More than half of healthcare organisations say their compliance spending has risen significantly – the highest proportion of any sector.
- 34,000+ European organisations, businesses and citizens were surveyed for AWS’ Unlocking Europe’s AI Potential report.
How important is a joined-up approach to AI regulation, and what would that look like in practice?
SR: It’s absolutely crucial. In practice, a joined-up approach means making it as simple as possible for organisations to understand and comply with the rules: one coherent framework, common definitions, and a clear point of contact for regulators across the EU.
Today, a founder can face different rules, different interpretations, and different regulatory bodies across 27 countries. That creates unnecessary complexity and can slow innovation. There are positive signs that this is being recognised.
The Commission’s simplification proposals are a step in the right direction - the challenge now is turning that ambition into a genuinely consistent approach across Europe.
What needs to change to move from successful pilots to widespread adoption?
SR: Moving from successful pilots to widespread AI adoption in healthcare requires Europe to address the structural challenges that prevent promising AI solutions made in Europe from scaling.
Regulation and enforcement need to be simplified, harmonised, and predictable across the EU single market and build on international standards to facilitate companies scaling.
Secondly, Europe needs to treat AI skills as key infrastructure, giving leaders, the workforce, and citizens the confidence to integrate AI into core workflows rather than leaving it as a side project.
Finally, Europe needs stronger routes to growth capital, procurement and international markets, alongside closer collaboration between government, industry and civil society.
The goal is not deregulation, but clear, simplified, and trusted rules and the conditions to turn innovation into sustained, measurable outcomes.
“The goal is not deregulation, but clear, simplified, and trusted rules and the conditions to turn innovation into sustained, measurable outcomes. ”
Are there European AI companies you think could enact real transformative change in healthcare?
SR: Europe has several AI companies that could drive genuinely transformative change in healthcare because they are addressing real clinical and patient-access challenges.
- Iktos, for example, combines generative AI with automated laboratory robotics to accelerate drug discovery, potentially reducing development timelines from years to months.
- Proximie is tackling inequalities in surgical care by connecting operating rooms, allowing specialists to support and train colleagues remotely in real time.
- myTomorrows uses AI to help patients and physicians navigate clinical trials and pre-approval treatments, improving access to therapies that might otherwise remain out of reach.
- And Callyope is using AI to identify early signs of mental-health relapse between appointments, enabling more preventative intervention.
Together, these companies demonstrate how Europe can translate AI, research and clinical expertise into measurable improvements in patient outcomes.
If you could change one thing about EU AI policy to support health startups scaling up, what would it be?
SR: If I could change one thing, it would be to make the rules simpler, clearer and more consistent across Europe. Not because regulation matters less, but because clarity gives innovators the confidence to move responsibly.
The opportunity is extraordinary. 39% of healthcare companies believe AI could fundamentally transform their industry. Imagine what that could mean: earlier diagnoses, faster drug discovery, more personalised care, and better outcomes for patients.
Europe has the talent, the research and the ambition to lead here. What we need is an environment that allows the people building these solutions to scale them. Ultimately, this isn't about AI.
It's about what AI makes possible for people - finding cures faster, giving doctors better tools, and giving patients more hope. The real job now is to make sure the best ideas don't stay ideas. They reach the people who need them most.

articles.full_text:
Moscow ordered Hungarian embassy and consulate staff out just weeks after Budapest expelled 10 Russian diplomats on national security grounds in September, the first such move by Hungary since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia expelled a group of Hungarian diplomats on Thursday after Hungary ordered 10 Russian diplomats out last month, marking a sharp break from the era of former Premier Viktor Orbán, who maintained closer ties with Moscow than any other EU leader.
Hungary's chargé d'affaires Gábor Gergics was summoned to Russia's foreign ministry and informed that staff from the Hungarian embassy in Moscow and consulates in St Petersburg and Kazan had been ordered to leave within two weeks.
Moscow described Hungary's original 8 September expulsion as a "baseless and openly unfriendly" act.
Budapest acknowledged Moscow's decision but said it stood by its position.
"Hungary is not interested in an escalation of diplomatic tensions. But we stand by our decision, taken on national security grounds. Our missions continue to operate in full, and Hungary will maintain its diplomatic presence in Russia," the Hungarian foreign ministry wrote on X.
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said at the time of the initial expulsion that the Russian diplomats "had been engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."
The mutual expulsions follow a shift in Hungarian foreign policy since Prime Minister Péter Magyar took office earlier this year.
At the end of August, the new government's guidance to its delegation at the UN General Assembly officially described Russia as a threat to Hungary and to the "global order," condemned its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and affirmed support for Ukrainian sovereignty and its right to self-defence.
Hungary is also seeking to improve relations with Kyiv, although Budapest is blocking the opening of new EU accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine to secure concessions on the rights of the country's Hungarian minority.
Orbán, who was in power for 16 years until his party Fidesz' loss in general elections this April, openly sympathised with the Kremlin and refused to join other EU member states in expelling Russian diplomats after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He made multiple visits to Moscow after the invasion and repeatedly used Hungary's veto in the European Council to block Ukraine-related initiatives.
Magyar has promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow during his tenure.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing strongly across Europe, with AI clusters emerging in major office markets and smaller academic and specialist hubs, according to new research from Colliers.
The report, AI Clusters in Europe: Where AI companies are growing and what it means for office demand, identifies London, Paris and Berlin as Europe’s leading AI clusters, attracting talent, investment and business expansion. A second tier of hubs is emerging in Munich, Zürich, Amsterdam, Dublin, Stockholm, Warsaw, Barcelona and Helsinki, while other cities are developing increasingly specialised AI ecosystems. Beyond these established hubs, Madrid, Milan and Copenhagen are emerging as specialised AI clusters, building on local academic expertise and established technology and industrial strengths.
Colliers’ analysis of AI clusters in Europe finds that the most successful bring together four critical ingredients: government-led initiatives, strong startup ecosystems, universities and research institutions, and Big Tech laboratories. Substantial data centre capacity provides an increasingly important supporting foundation.
London and Paris are the only European AI clusters that currently combine all four ingredients at scale, supported by significant data centre capacity. Berlin has developed a different model, driven by its startup culture, engineering talent and distributed network of entrepreneurial and research-led districts.
The research also points to significant economic potential. AI is expected to increase European GDP by around 10% to 11% by 2030 through productivity gains, automation and the creation of new products and services. The EU’s strategic challenge is not primarily a lack of innovation, but its ability to commercialise research, attract investment and build globally competitive AI businesses.
The impact is already becoming visible in occupational markets. AI businesses are creating demand directly as they recruit and expand, while the adoption of AI is also driving transformation across existing office-based sectors.
The report identifies a new type of occupier: highly capitalised, exceptionally fast-growing AI businesses that recruit aggressively and can outgrow their premises within a relatively short period. Many initially use serviced or flexible offices before moving into larger permanent premises, making their full real estate footprint difficult to capture through conventional leasing data.
London provides the clearest current example. AI businesses accounted for 19% of total London office take-up in the second quarter of 2026, up from 10% in the previous quarter. Colliers notes that London may be an outlier in scale, but its experience illustrates the potential effect on other European markets as their AI clusters mature.
For investors and developers, the growth of AI brings both a demand opportunity and a product challenge. The report finds that the buildings best placed to attract AI occupiers are likely to combine strong locations, high-capacity digital and power infrastructure, flexible layouts, collaboration space and the ability to accommodate rapid growth.
Although AI’s long-term effect on employment and real estate remains uncertain, Colliers concludes that it is already reinforcing demand for high-quality offices and digital infrastructure in Europe’s most talent-rich cities.
Damian Harrington, Head of Research, Global Capital Markets & EMEA at Colliers, said: “AI is rapidly becoming an economic geography and real estate story. Its growth is reinforcing the importance of cities that can bring together specialist talent, research, capital, infrastructure and enterprise customers.”
Harrington added: “The implications extend well beyond the technology sector. The cities that develop successful AI ecosystems will be better placed to attract investment, create high-value employment and secure new sources of office demand.”
Karin Witalis, Associate Director, Commercial Real Estate, EMEA Research at Colliers, said: “AI businesses are not choosing locations on cost alone. Access to highly skilled people, universities, research institutions, venture capital and established technology networks is central to their decisions.”
Witalis continued: “This is helping to reinforce successful metropolitan ecosystems and the innovation districts within them. It also creates an opportunity for European cities with strong academic or specialist foundations to build distinctive positions within the wider AI economy.”

EUR/GBP trades on the defensive on Thursday, remaining on the back foot for the fifth consecutive day following last week’s rejection from the 0.8600 psychological mark. At the time of writing, the cross trades around 0.8537, its lowest level since mid-August.
The British Pound (GBP) strengthened across the board on Wednesday after UK second-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was revised higher to 0.5% QoQ from 0.4%, while the annual growth rate was raised to 1.4% from 1.2%.
