articles.title: 🌊 Far-right setbacks do not reverse illiberal change - theloop.ecpr.eu
articles.summary: 🌊 Far-right setbacks do not reverse illiberal change  theloop.ecpr.eu
articles.full_text:
Sweden's recent election defeated the right-wing Tidö bloc and blocked the populist Sweden Democrats' route into government. Yet the restrictive political settlement they helped construct may endure. Vera Tika argues that far-right normalisation is not automatically reversed by electoral defeat: once institutionalised, illiberal change can acquire a political life of its own
Sweden's election interrupted Europe's wider rightward movement. The final count gave the opposition parties 176 seats, against 173 for the right-wing Tidö bloc. The Sweden Democrats fell to 17.5% and 62 seats, dropping from second to third place. Their anticipated transition from external support to cabinet participation was therefore blocked. But the election did not return Sweden to the political landscape that preceded their rise.
Since 2022, the Sweden Democrats have supported Ulf Kristersson's minority government through the Tidö Agreement. From outside the cabinet, they helped move migration, citizenship, policing and criminal justice towards a more restrictive settlement. Kristersson has resigned, but forming a new government will require negotiations among opposition parties with substantial policy differences. The Social Democrats have also adapted to demands for tighter migration controls. Electoral defeat has weakened the Sweden Democrats' parliamentary leverage, but it has not removed the political assumptions they helped normalise.
Political scientists distinguish the populist radical right from the extreme right. The former combines nativism – the belief that the state belongs to a culturally homogeneous native group – with authoritarianism and, often, populism. It challenges liberal pluralism but ordinarily competes through elections. Its power therefore cannot be measured only through votes, seats or ministerial office.
Mainstreaming and normalisation describe different stages of that power. Mainstreaming concerns what established parties and media do: adopt positions, repeat frames, cooperate or treat former pariahs as legitimate competitors. Normalisation is the outcome; a shifted threshold of acceptability. Institutionalisation follows when these ideas shape legislation, administrative routines and policy instruments.
Far-right parties exercise issue ownership: they make migration, security and identity the terrain on which others feel compelled to compete
Far-right parties also exercise issue ownership: they make migration, security and identity the terrain on which others feel compelled to compete. Accommodation can therefore strengthen rather than displace them. Once mainstream actors preserve the same problem definitions, influence survives electoral defeat. Sweden reveals this political sedimentation: the party loses ground, while the policy settlement remains.
Italy demonstrates the same process from inside government. Its radical-right Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, has cultivated an image of institutional reliability. Her government has remained anchored in NATO and EU fiscal constraints, while continuing to support Ukraine. These choices are often presented as evidence that responsibility moderates the radical right.
Meloni's goverment may remain anchored in NATO and EU fiscal constraints, yet it has proposed banning face veils in schools and limiting the number of foreign pupils per classroom
Yet moderation is not a single movement affecting every policy field equally. International pragmatism can coexist with illiberal change at home. In September, Meloni proposed banning face veils in schools and limiting foreign pupils per classroom. The European Commission's 2026 Rule of Law Report also records concerns involving media pluralism, institutional checks and civic space in Italy.
Meloni's trajectory is better understood as differentiated normalisation. Radical-right actors may moderate where credibility with markets, allies or EU institutions is indispensable. At the same time, they can retain exclusionary conceptions of membership and expand executive discretion at home. Respectability in one domain can make transformation in another less visible.
Germany illustrates both the reach and the limits of electoral containment. The Federal Republic's postwar order combined militant-democratic safeguards with a party-system norm excluding the far right. The Brandmauer is today's cordon sanitaire: it denies the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) coalition partners. Yet after winning almost 44% in Saxony-Anhalt, AfD came first in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 38.3%, while the Christian Democratic Union fell below the 5% threshold for the first time in a state election. Together, these results mark a rupture in postwar containment: the AfD is now the largest party in several Länder even while excluded from office. Berlin qualifies, but does not reverse, this pattern. Die Linke won by centring housing, while AfD achieved its best result in the capital, with 16.3%. The firewall still blocks office. But it no longer contains electoral growth, issue ownership or pressure on mainstream competitors.
In France, Rassemblement National's long strategy of normalisation has made it appear increasingly plausible as a governing party
France faces a related process ahead of its 2027 presidential election. Rassemblement National's long strategy of normalisation has made it appear increasingly plausible as a governing party. This affects competitors before it wins executive power. Policies and rhetoric are adjusted in anticipation of its strength, narrowing the distance between exclusion from office and influence over the political field.
These cases represent different configurations: external support in Sweden, direct government in Italy, electoral containment in Germany and anticipatory accommodation in France. What connects them is that far-right influence travels beyond the organisational boundaries of far-right parties.
Sweden's election remains significant. It ended the Tidö bloc's mandate, prevented the Sweden Democrats from converting policy influence into ministerial authority, and showed that far-right advance is not inevitable. Yet a change of government is not the same as a reversal of the policy and administrative changes made since 2022.
Democratic resilience must therefore be assessed at two levels. The first is whether radical-right parties gain office. The second is whether their definitions of belonging, threat and legitimate exclusion continue to organise public policy after they lose. Elections can remove parties from power. They do not automatically remove the political world those parties helped to build.

articles.title: “Biggest threat yet”: New EU rules could severely restrict online gaming - Notebookcheck
articles.summary: “Biggest threat yet”: New EU rules could severely restrict online gaming  Notebookcheck
articles.full_text:
Stop Killing Games is an initiative that aims to prevent purchased games from becoming permanently unplayable once publishers shut down their servers. However, a new EU legislative proposal could jeopardize that goal. On September 17, 2026, the European Commission officially presented the EU KIDS Act. It is intended to better protect minors when using digital services and explicitly covers online games alongside social networks, video platforms and AI chatbots. Among other things, the proposal includes stronger safeguards and age-verification procedures. The proposal still needs to be considered by the European Parliament and the Council.
Even before the official presentation, a version of the legislative proposal was leaked. Stop Killing Games has now taken a closer look at it – and reaches a stark assessment in an accompanying video. In the video, the speaker describes the KIDS Act as the “biggest threat yet” to Stop Killing Games' stated goal. The EU KIDS Act sets out strict requirements for online services. The main cause for concern is the very broad definition of online games and the obligations associated with it.
According to Stop Killing Games' interpretation, the rules could apply not only to traditional live-service or multiplayer titles, but also to games with individual online features – such as leaderboards, downloadable updates or privately operated servers. The video even raises concerns that virtually any digitally distributed game could be treated as an online service. However, the speaker acknowledges that the proposal is not clearly worded on this point.
Age verification for all online games, the end of private servers?
Stop Killing Games is particularly critical of the planned age-verification requirements. Simply entering a date of birth will likely no longer be sufficient. Instead, providers could be required to use more reliable age-verification methods before users are allowed to access certain online features. Stop Killing Games therefore fears that players could be required to provide personal information – and that this might not only apply to major platforms such as Steam, but potentially even to individual games.
The potential consequences for private servers could be just as drastic. If the operator of such a server is legally treated as a provider of an online game, they would also have to comply with the new protection and age requirements. Stop Killing Games sees this as directly conflicting with its own goal: If an official server is shut down, fans could technically keep an older game alive by running their own servers, but according to the initiative's interpretation, doing so could expose them to legal risks. In the video, the speaker cites Minecraft and Unreal Tournament as examples.
Would it still be worthwhile for developers to offer online games in the EU?
Another potentially significant issue is the possible cost for developers. Age verification, additional safeguards and other compliance requirements could place a considerable financial burden on smaller studios. The speaker criticizes the proposal for, in his view, not providing a general exemption for small developers. In the worst-case scenario, studios could therefore decide not to offer online games in the EU at all.
However, this interpretation is far from definitive. The video repeatedly acknowledges that some of the wording is difficult to interpret and that even lawyers consulted on the matter did not agree on every point. The potential consequences described here should therefore explicitly not be understood as established law, but rather as Stop Killing Games' warning about the possible effects of the proposed legislation.

articles.title: How to prepare for the looming energy crisis - The Telegraph
articles.summary: How to prepare for the looming energy crisis  The TelegraphHousehold energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years  BBCMillions to spend this winter in cold homes if government fails to cap killer energy price hikes  Morning Star | The People’s DailyWe need a fix for the UK’s energy market, not a blanket giveaway  The TimesEnergy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has warned British households face an energy crisis this winter, with bills poised to soar to almost £2,000 a year from January.
Conflict in the Middle East has disrupted gas supplies since March, depleting stocks across Europe and pushing up energy costs in Britain.
Around 22 million households with tariffs dictated by the most recent energy price cap, in place from Oct 1 to Dec 31, will see a 4pc increase in their energy bills, which amounts to around £60 a year on average.
For a dual fuel customer, using both gas and electricity, the typical annual bill now stands at £1,723. This is in spite of Mr Burnham removing VAT from electricity bills until the end of March.
But Cornwall Insight, an energy consultancy, has predicted that bills will increase steeply in January. Household costs are set to rise by a further 16pc at the start of 2027, equivalent to an extra £276 on the typical bill, which is predicted to reach £1,999.
Dr Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said: “These prices are going to hit households hard.
“January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas, and now they face the biggest price cap rise we’ve seen in four years. At the moment, we can’t yet see an end to the volatility.”
Here, Telegraph Money examines what you can do to prepare for the coming squeeze.
Fix your energy tariff
Customers on a fixed energy tariff will be protected from any further rises to the price cap.
Signing up to a deal with a locked-in price now could protect you from soaring gas and electricity prices throughout most of 2027. Instead, fluctuations to your bill will depend on your energy usage.
Energy suppliers often offer a fix of at least 12 months below the current price cap. Given that bills are set to rise further in January, and possibly beyond, taking up that sort of offer now is likely to save you money over the next year.
At present, the best deal on the market is an 18-month fix from Fuse Energy, according to comparison website Uswitch. The tariff equates to an annual bill of £1,612 a year, which is £111 below the October price cap.

articles.summary: UK house price growth halves amid rising mortgage interest rates  The GuardianUK house prices fall as higher mortgage rates ‘subdue’ market  Financial TimesUK house prices fall unexpectedly as buyers brace for interest rate rises  The TelegraphUK house prices slowed unexpectedly in September  The TimesAutumn Budget: property in a changing Britain  coutts.com
articles.full_text:
Annual house price growth halved in the UK last month, as economic uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East continued to deter homebuyers.
The average price of a British home rose 0.8% in the year to September to £274,251, according to Nationwide. That was half the rate recorded in August, when house prices grew 1.6% year on year. It also marked the slowest pace of home price growth since December last year.
House prices across the UK fell 0.2% month on month, after taking account of seasonal effects.
The housing market has been subdued in recent months, as the US-Israel war with Iran and resulting disruption to Gulf oil and gas flows drive up energy costs and inflation fears. That has fed through to higher interest rates on mortgages, making it more expensive for people to buy new homes.
“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns,” the Nationwide chief economist, Robert Gardner, said.
“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank [of England] rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.”
Moneyfacts reported earlier this week that the average interest rate on a two-year fixed mortgage in the UK had risen to its highest level since July 2024, while the average rate on a five-year fixed rate mortgage hit its highest level since October 2023. Both were sitting above 5.9%.
That could rise further, given that investors are pricing in a 92% chance that the Bank of England will raise interest rates, from 3.75% to 4%, at its next meeting on 5 November. Markets expect the Bank to institute at least three further rises in 2027, taking the base rate to 4.75% by the end of next year.
Threadneedle Street is trying to bring inflation, now at 3.1%, back down to its 2% target. However, it predicted last month that the consumer price index of inflation could rise above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.
Nationwide said that across the regions East Anglia posted the biggest hit to house prices, logging an annual decline of 0.7%. Northern Ireland was an exception, experiencing the strongest house price growth at an annual rate of 5.9%.
The house price slowdown has improved affordability for some homebuyers, Gardner said.
“Underlying affordability is improving, as house price growth has been well below earnings growth for some time,” he said. “These gains have been only partially offset by higher mortgage rates. This suggests that activity should regain momentum in the quarters ahead, providing the energy shock fades and confidence returns – especially if market interest rates fall back to pre-conflict levels.”
Meanwhile, prospective homeowners are preparing for the launch of the government’s Your First Home scheme, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”.
The scheme involves a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price, with the buyer having to put down a minimum deposit of only 2.5%, which meanings taking out a standard mortgage for just 77.5% of the property’s value.
The scheme applies only to England and new-build flats or houses. News of its launch has already increased the share price of housebuilders including Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, Taylor Wimpey, Crest Nicholson and Vistry.

articles.title: New rules on the right to work for people applying for international protection
articles.summary: The new Reception Act comes into force on 1 October. Among other things, it changes the rules on when a person applying for international protection (asylum) has the right to work.
articles.full_text:
New rules on the right to work for people applying for international protection
The new Reception Act comes into force on 1 October. Among other things, it changes the rules on when a person applying for international protection (asylum) has the right to work.
From 1 October, a person applying for international protection (asylum) may be granted access to the labour market (previously known as AT-UND, an exemption from the work permit requirement) if the Swedish Migration Agency has not made a decision within six months of the application being registered. To be granted the right to work, the delay must not be due to the applicant and the other conditions must also be met.
People who already have AT-UND will keep it
As a general rule, anyone who already has AT-UND when the new Reception Act comes into force will keep their exemption and can therefore continue to work. However, in some cases an existing AT-UND may cease to apply. As an employer, you therefore still need to check that the person has the right to work.
Information about the right to work is available on the application card
Everyone who has submitted an application for international protection (asylum) receives an application card from the Swedish Migration Agency. The application card replaces the previous LMA card, and by 1 October at the latest, everyone who has applied for international protection should have received the new card.
The application card has a QR code. As an employer, you can scan the QR code to check
- whether the card is valid
- whether the person has AT-UND
- how long the person’s AT-UND is valid for.
The information displayed via the QR code is up to date when the code is scanned. It is therefore important to check the card even if the person has previously shown that they have AT-UND.
People from Ukraine seeking protection are not affected
The change to the right to work only applies to people applying for international protection (asylum). People from Ukraine who have been granted temporary protection under the Temporary Protection Directive are not affected. They have the same right to work in Sweden as before, as a permit under the Temporary Protection Directive also includes a work permit.
Read more about employing a person who is applying for international protection

articles.title: New Reception Act comes into force on 1 October
articles.summary: A new Reception Act comes into force on 1 October. It replaces the Act on Reception of Asylum Seekers (LMA). Among other things, the new Act means that more people will be covered by the Swedish Migration Agency’s reception system and introduces new rules on geographical restrictions and control measures.
articles.full_text:
New Reception Act comes into force on 1 October
A new Reception Act comes into force on 1 October. It replaces the Act on Reception of Asylum Seekers (LMA). Among other things, the new Act means that more people will be covered by the Swedish Migration Agency’s reception system and introduces new rules on geographical restrictions and control measures.
Under the new Reception Act, more people can be covered by the Act and some will be covered for longer than before.
One important change concerns people who have received an enforceable return decision. They can continue to be covered by the Reception Act even after the decision has come into effect or the time limit for voluntary departure has expired. There will also be more opportunities for people who were previously no longer covered by the reception system to be covered again.
Geographical restrictions and control measures are introduced
As a general rule, people applying for international protection (asylum) are already required to live in accommodation assigned to them by the Swedish Migration Agency. From 1 October, a geographical restriction will be introduced. As a general rule, people applying for international protection and people who have received a return decision must remain within the county where their assigned accommodation is located.
Attendance checks will also be introduced at the Swedish Migration Agency’s reception and return centres. People aged 16 or over who are applying for international protection and living at a centre must attend these checks on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
People who have received a return decision will also be required to report to the Swedish Migration Agency. As a general rule, they must report three days a week. In certain situations, the Swedish Migration Agency may also decide on other individual control measures.
People from Ukraine who have temporary protection under the Temporary Protection Directive are not subject to the geographical restriction or attendance checks.
More requirements linked to the daily allowance
The daily allowance can already be reduced if a person does not meet certain requirements. Under the new Reception Act, there will be more situations in which the daily allowance can be reduced, either in full or in part.
This includes situations where a person does not follow their geographical restriction or does not report to the Swedish Migration Agency as required. The daily allowance can also be reduced in cases of serious misconduct at accommodation provided by the Swedish Migration Agency.
Another change is that the Swedish Migration Agency can require repayment of daily allowance that has been paid incorrectly.
The right to work will be restricted
From 1 October, the rules on when a person applying for international protection may be granted access to the labour market will also change. This was previously known as an exemption from the work permit requirement (AT-UND). As a general rule, a person will only be granted the right to work if the Swedish Migration Agency has not made a decision on their application within six months of the date on which the application was registered. The delay must not be due to the applicant and the other conditions must also be met.
People from Ukraine and people who already have AT-UND are not affected
As a general rule, people who already have AT-UND when the new Reception Act comes into force will keep it and can continue to work.
The new rules on AT-UND do not affect people from Ukraine who have temporary protection under the Temporary Protection Directive.
Municipalities’ responsibilities are clarified
The new Reception Act changes how responsibilities are divided between the Swedish Migration Agency and municipalities. The Act clarifies municipalities’ responsibilities for providing support and assistance in accommodation, as well as special forms of accommodation, for people covered by the Reception Act. This may, for example, include home care services for a person living at one of the Swedish Migration Agency’s centres.
New rules are also being introduced on municipalities’ responsibility for providing accommodation in an extraordinary situation where large numbers of people seek protection.

articles.title: New rules for young adults and people who want to move to a family member in Sweden
articles.summary: The Swedish Parliament has adopted new rules on immigration due to family ties that come into force on 1 October 2026. Among other changes, certain young adults who previously held a residence permit on the grounds of family ties will be able to apply for a residence permit from within Sweden. The rules also affect people who want to move to a family member in Sweden and people who want to extend their residence permit to continue living with a family member in Sweden.
articles.full_text:
New rules for young adults and people who want to move to a family member in Sweden
The Swedish Parliament has adopted new rules on immigration due to family ties that come into force on 1 October 2026. Among other changes, certain young adults who previously held a residence permit on the grounds of family ties will be able to apply for a residence permit from within Sweden. The rules also affect people who want to move to a family member in Sweden and people who want to extend their residence permit to continue living with a family member in Sweden.
In March this year, the Swedish Migration Agency announced that decisions to reject applications in certain cases involving young adults who previously held a residence permit on the grounds of family ties had been put on hold after the Government announced that new legislation was being prepared. These cases concern people who previously held a residence permit on the grounds of family ties to a parent but have since turned 18.
– The Swedish Migration Agency is now resuming its examination of the cases that were put on hold. Our aim is to ensure that all young adults have the opportunity to apply for a residence permit and have their application examined without the Agency’s processing time affecting the outcome,” says Ann-Kari Olsson, Head of Section at the Swedish Migration Agency.
The new rules coming into force allow young adults to apply for an extension of their residence permit on the grounds of family ties to their parents even after they have turned 18. During a transitional period, certain young adults who have already received an expulsion decision will also be covered.
A temporary opportunity is also being introduced to apply for a permit on other grounds without first having to leave Sweden. This will apply until the end of December 2027.
– It is important to emphasise that this temporary opportunity allows them to apply for a permit on other grounds from within Sweden, but they must meet the requirements for that permit. No special requirements apply,” says Ann-Kari Olsson.
Residence requirement and stricter maintenance requirement
Several conditions for family immigration are also being tightened. Among other changes, a requirement is being introduced that, as a general rule, a person in Sweden who holds a temporary residence permit and whom a family member wishes to join must have resided in Sweden for at least two years when the family member applies for a residence permit.
The two-year period of residence requirement does not apply to people with work permits, researchers, doctoral students, people with EU Blue Cards or ICT permits, or unaccompanied minors and their parents. They are covered by other rules.
Refugees may also be exempt from the requirement in certain situations.
The stricter maintenance requirement means that the amount the person in Sweden must have left after paying their housing costs will increase. The maintenance requirement must also be met when a family member applies for an extension of their residence permit. In such cases, the family member’s income can normally also be taken into account.
“The Swedish Migration Agency has carried out extensive work in preparation for the new rules. This includes analysing what the rules mean for our examination of cases and adapting procedures, working methods, policy and guidance documents, and information,” says Ann-Kari Olsson.
